posts.title: MCP Prompts: The Template Only the User Can Trigger
posts.subtitle: The third MCP primitive — not model-invoked, not app-curated, but explicitly picked by a person
posts.summary: MCP Prompts let a server ship reusable, parameterized prompt templates that a user explicitly selects — like a slash command — rather than something the model decides to call (Tools) or the app quietly attaches (Resources). A client fetches the filled-in template via prompts/get and hands the result straight to the model, so good prompting becomes something a server ships once instead of something every user has to reinvent.

slides.title: Not every good prompt should be reinvented by hand
slides.body: MCP Prompts let a server package a well-tuned prompt template once, so a user can trigger it explicitly instead of retyping a careful instruction every time.

slides.title: Good prompting doesn't scale as tribal knowledge
slides.body: The person who knows exactly how to phrase a request to a tool-rich server isn't always the one using it.
bullets: A server with a dozen Tools and Resources still needs the user to phrase the right request — "review this PR for security issues, checking auth and input validation" is easy to get vague or forget entirely
Copy-pasted prompt snippets drift out of sync as the server's capabilities change underneath them
MCP Tools are model-invoked and Resources are typically app-curated — neither primitive gives a human a direct, explicit "run this exact interaction" affordance

slides.title: Prompts: parameterized templates, explicitly picked
slides.body: A server declares a catalog of named prompts; a client turns a user's selection into ready-to-send messages.
bullets: prompts/list returns each prompt's name, title, description, and its arguments (name, description, whether required)
prompts/get takes a name plus argument values and returns a list of messages — role and content — ready to send to the model
A prompt's messages can embed resource content directly (e.g. a file's text) so the user doesn't have to manually attach anything alongside it
Servers can declare a completions capability so a client can offer autocomplete while a user types an argument value

slides.title: User-controlled — the third control plane
slides.body: MCP deliberately splits control three ways, one primitive per decision-maker.
bullets: Tools: the model decides when to call them, based on the conversation
Resources: the application typically decides what gets attached to context
Prompts: the user explicitly selects them — commonly surfaced as a slash command or menu pick in a client's UI
Because a Prompt is explicitly triggered, it's visible to the user by definition — it's not a channel for hiding instructions from them

slides.title: Worked example: /review-pr in a coding client
slides.body: A single server-defined prompt replaces a paragraph the user would otherwise retype every time.
bullets: A GitHub MCP server declares a prompt named review-pr with one argument: pr_number (required)
A user picks /review-pr from their client's command menu and enters 482
The client calls prompts/get with { name: "review-pr", arguments: { pr_number: "482" } }

The server returns messages that embed the actual diff plus a tuned instruction ("check for security issues, missing tests, and style violations") — the model receives a complete, well-formed request without the user writing a word of it

slides.title: Prompts vs. Tools vs. Resources
slides.body: Same protocol, three different jobs and three different decision-makers.

rows: May be invisible to the user

slides.title: Pitfalls: Prompts aren't a guaranteed or catch-all channel
slides.body: Support is optional, and Prompts solve a specific problem — not every prompting need.
bullets: Prompt support is an optional MCP capability; a client that doesn't implement it never shows the server's prompts at all, no matter how useful they are
Too many near-duplicate prompts clutter a picker the same way an overloaded Tools list clutters a model's decision-making — curate the catalog, don't dump every possible template into it
Required arguments should be validated by the server in prompts/get — a client shouldn't have to guess whether "pr_number" needs to be a string or an int before calling it
Prompts are for interactions a human deliberately starts; if the model itself needs to decide dynamically what to fetch or do mid-conversation, that's what Tools are for, not a Prompt

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Prompts are MCP's user-invoked primitive: reusable, parameterized templates a person explicitly selects, distinct from Tools (model-invoked) and Resources (app-curated)
prompts/list discovers the catalog; prompts/get fills in arguments and returns ready-to-send messages, which can embed resource content directly
Because a user explicitly triggers a Prompt, it's inherently visible — it complements Tools and Resources rather than replacing either
Support is optional per client — don't rely on Prompts for anything critical unless you've confirmed your target host actually surfaces them

questions.prompt: What distinguishes MCP Prompts from Tools and Resources in terms of who invokes them?
options: Prompts are invoked by the model, just like Tools
Prompts are explicitly selected by the user — unlike Tools (model-invoked) and Resources (typically app-curated)
Prompts are invoked automatically by the server itself, with no client involvement
There's no difference — all three primitives are invoked identically
questions.explanation: MCP splits control three ways: the model decides when to call a Tool, the application typically decides what Resources get attached, and a human user explicitly selects a Prompt — commonly via a slash command or menu.

questions.prompt: What does a client receive back from a prompts/get call?
options: A raw file the user must manually copy into the chat
A list of ready-to-send messages (role and content), which can embed resource content directly
Only a boolean indicating whether the prompt exists
The full source code of the MCP server
questions.explanation: prompts/get takes a prompt name and argument values and returns a list of messages — already formed with role and content — ready to send to the model, potentially with resource content embedded inline.

questions.prompt: Why is a Prompt not a good channel for hiding instructions from the user?
options: MCP technically forbids servers from writing prompt content
A Prompt requires the user to explicitly select and trigger it, so by definition the user is aware it's being used
Prompts are encrypted and cannot contain instructions at all
Only Tools are capable of carrying instructions
questions.explanation: Since a human deliberately picks and triggers a Prompt — typically via a visible slash command or menu — the interaction is inherently visible to them, unlike a Tool call the model might make without the user noticing.

posts.title: Circuit Breakers: Stopping Cascading Failure
posts.subtitle: The pattern that trips before one slow dependency drags down everything upstream
posts.summary: Circuit breakers stop a struggling downstream service from taking the whole system down by failing fast instead of piling up retries. This post covers the closed/open/half-open state machine, real Hystrix-era thresholds, how it pairs with timeouts and bulkheads, and the thundering-herd trap a misconfigured half-open state creates.

slides.title: One Slow Service, One System-Wide Outage
slides.body: A payment API starts timing out. Callers retry. Threads pile up waiting on responses that never come. Within minutes, an unrelated part of the system is down too — not because it failed, but because it ran out of threads waiting on something that did.
bullets: Cascading failure is a resource-exhaustion problem, not a logic bug
Circuit breakers stop the bleeding by refusing to call a dependency that's already failing
Popularized by Netflix's Hystrix after real cascading outages in production

slides.title: Why Retries and Timeouts Alone Aren't Enough
slides.body: Timeouts cap how long you wait per call, but if every caller still tries every request, you just get slow failures instead of fast ones — and the thread or connection pool still drains.
bullets: A 500ms timeout with retries under heavy load still exhausts a fixed-size thread pool in seconds
Retries amplify load on a struggling service exactly when it needs less traffic
The failure spreads upstream: caller A blocks on B, caller Z blocks on A

slides.title: Three States: Closed, Open, Half-Open
slides.body: A circuit breaker wraps each call to a dependency and tracks its own health, switching behavior based on the recent failure rate.
bullets: Closed: requests flow normally; breaker counts failures in a rolling window
Open: once failures cross a threshold, every call fails immediately (fail-fast) without touching the dependency
Half-Open: after a cool-down, a small number of trial requests test whether the dependency recovered
Hystrix's classic defaults: at least 20 requests and a 50% error rate in a 10s window trips it open, then a 5s sleep window before half-open

slides.title: Where It Sits in the Call Path
slides.body: The breaker lives on the caller's side, per dependency — not inside the service being called.
bullets: Each downstream dependency gets its own breaker instance and its own thread pool or semaphore (a bulkhead)
Stacks with timeouts (cap wait per call) and retries (used sparingly, only on the closed path)
Library-level tools (resilience4j, Polly, Hystrix) track state per process; service-mesh level (Envoy, Istio) tracks it per proxy sidecar instead
The open state should trigger a fallback — cached data, a default value, a degraded response — not just a raw exception

slides.title: Checkout Without the Fraud Service
slides.body: A checkout flow calls a fraud-scoring service before confirming payment. The fraud service starts timing out under load.
bullets: Requests 1–20: normal fraud checks, breaker closed, quietly counting a rising error rate
Request 21: error rate crosses the 50% threshold in the rolling window — breaker flips open
Requests 22+: checkout skips the fraud call entirely, falls back to a conservative rule-based score, keeps selling
After the sleep window, one trial request probes the fraud service; if it succeeds, the breaker closes and normal checks resume

slides.title: Circuit Breaker vs. Its Neighbors
slides.body: These patterns are complementary, not competitors — production systems typically run all four together.

rows: Waiting forever on one slow call
One request fails after N ms
Too short: false failures; too long: still ties up threads
Amplifies load on an already-struggling service
Repeated failure taking down the caller
Fails instantly, no network call made
Too loose: cascades anyway; too tight: flaps on normal noise
Too many pools: resource waste; too few: isolation doesn't hold

slides.title: When It Backfires
slides.body: A circuit breaker adds a failure mode of its own if the thresholds or topology aren't tuned.
bullets: Thundering herd: many replicas going half-open at the same instant re-flood a barely-recovering dependency — jitter the trial timing or share breaker state
Per-instance state in a horizontally scaled fleet means each replica trips independently; one hot replica's trouble doesn't always show up on the others
Thresholds set too aggressively trip on normal noise ("flapping"); set too loosely, they never trip before real damage happens
A breaker with no fallback just turns one failure into a different, faster failure — it doesn't fix availability by itself

slides.title: The Core Idea
bullets: Circuit breakers trade a slow, resource-draining failure for a fast, cheap one
The state machine is simple — closed → open → half-open — but the thresholds and fallback are where the real engineering is
Always pair it with a fallback path; failing fast with no fallback just moves the outage upstream
In a fleet of replicas, decide deliberately whether breaker state is per-instance or shared — it changes the failure shape

questions.prompt: After a circuit breaker's failure threshold is crossed, what does it do in the Open state?
options: Keeps forwarding every request as before
Fails every call immediately without contacting the dependency
Doubles the timeout on each retry
Queues requests until the dependency recovers
questions.explanation: Open means fail-fast: the breaker stops sending requests to the struggling dependency entirely, protecting the caller's own threads and connections instead of tying them up waiting on calls that are likely to fail.

questions.prompt: Hystrix's classic default thresholds required which condition before tripping a circuit open?
options: A single failed request
At least 20 requests and a 50% error rate within a 10-second window
A 99% error rate sustained for 24 hours
Any request slower than 100ms
questions.explanation: Requiring a minimum request volume (20) and a real error rate (50%) in a short rolling window keeps a single blip from prematurely opening the breaker, while still reacting within seconds to a genuine outage.

questions.prompt: In a fleet of 50 service replicas, each running its own circuit breaker, what commonly goes wrong when they all transition to half-open at once?
options: Nothing — half-open state doesn't send any traffic
Their simultaneous trial requests can re-overwhelm a dependency that was just starting to recover
The breakers permanently lock into the open state
Half-open automatically load-balances trials across regions
questions.explanation: Per-instance breaker state means 50 replicas can all decide to test the dependency in the same instant, turning a gentle recovery probe into a burst of load — the same thundering-herd problem the breaker was meant to prevent. Jittering the sleep window or sharing breaker state avoids it.

bullets: No lab name attached — just strong, unexplained performance

posts.title: VoiceMem: Giving Voice Agents a Memory That Keeps Up
posts.subtitle: A dual-brain memory architecture built for the 200ms turn-taking budget of live speech
posts.summary: Researchers from Nanyang Technological University (with Shuicheng Yan among the authors) introduce VoiceMem, a streaming dual-brain memory for spoken language models that splits factual and emotional recall into separate paths and completes retrieval in 134ms — fast enough not to break a live conversation.

slides.title: Voice Agents Forget Mid-Conversation
slides.body: Text chatbots can pause a beat to search memory. A voice agent can't — silence past a few hundred milliseconds reads as broken.
bullets: Real-time duplex speech needs a reply within roughly 200ms of the user finishing
Most memory systems (RAG-style stores like Mem0) were designed for text turns, not live audio
Paper: "VoiceMem: Streaming Dual-Brain Memory for Real-Time Interaction" (Xie, Yan, et al., NTU Singapore, Aug 2026)

slides.title: The Latency Wall
slides.body: Bolting a classic retrieval-augmented memory onto a speech model breaks the conversation in two distinct ways.
bullets: Batch-style retrieval (encode the whole turn, then search) adds seconds, not milliseconds
A single memory store conflates "what was said" with "how they felt about it"
Losing emotional/persona continuity makes long-horizon companionship or support use cases feel amnesiac

slides.title: Two Brains, One Stream
slides.body: VoiceMem runs two specialized memory paths in parallel and writes/reads them incrementally as audio streams in, instead of waiting for a full turn to end.
bullets: Left brain: informational memory — facts, structured retrieval
Right brain: emotional/persona memory — tone, preferences, relationship history
Streaming memory I/O: both update and query continuously, not in one batch step
Deployed with interchangeable memory backends, decoupled from the core model

slides.title: What Splitting Memory Buys You

rows: state of the art on 3 persona benchmarks

slides.title: A Concrete Turn
slides.body: Mid-call, a user references something emotionally loaded from a conversation weeks earlier.
bullets: Left brain streams a fact check (what exactly was discussed) in parallel with audio input
Right brain surfaces the prior emotional context (how they reacted, what tone worked)
Both resolve inside the 134ms budget, so the spoken reply doesn't stall
Because backends are interchangeable, a product team can swap the underlying vector store without retraining the model

slides.title: Where Dual-Brain Memory Strains
slides.body: Splitting memory into two systems is a real engineering and evaluation tradeoff, not a free win.
bullets: Two stores can drift out of sync — a fact update doesn't automatically update the emotional read on it
More moving parts than a single unified memory store
Gains are largest for long-horizon, emotionally-loaded use cases; overkill for a one-shot voice IVR lookup
Reported gains are on the authors' own persona benchmarks — independent third-party replication is still pending

slides.title: Why It Matters
bullets: Real-time voice memory needs sub-200ms retrieval — standard RAG latency doesn't fit
Separating factual from emotional memory measurably improved both in this study
Streaming I/O beats "encode the full turn, then retrieve" for live audio
Interchangeable backends matter for actually shipping this in production voice products

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Buying Accuracy With Inference FLOPs
posts.subtitle: Why 2026's flagship models ship a "thinking effort" dial instead of one fixed forward pass
posts.summary: Test-time compute scaling spends extra inference-time computation — longer reasoning, multiple sampled attempts, or guided search — to squeeze more accuracy out of a fixed model, trading latency and cost for correctness on a per-query basis.

slides.title: More Thinking, Better Answers — At a Price
slides.body: Instead of only scaling training compute (bigger models, more data), labs increasingly scale inference compute: let the model "think" longer on a given query.
bullets: 2026 flagship releases increasingly expose an explicit thinking-effort knob (e.g. High / Max) instead of one fixed pass
Same weights, same model — the only thing that changes is how much compute you spend per request

slides.title: Why a Bigger Model Isn't Always the Answer
slides.body: Training-time scaling hits diminishing returns and costs millions of dollars per run before you even serve a single query.
bullets: A fixed-size model given more "time to think" on a hard problem can match or beat a much larger model — on that problem
But every extra reasoning token is billed and adds latency — it's a per-query dial, not a free upgrade
The right amount of "thinking" varies wildly by task difficulty

slides.title: How the Extra Compute Gets Spent
slides.body: Three broad families of test-time compute, each spending the extra FLOPs differently.
bullets: Longer chain-of-thought: more intermediate reasoning tokens before the final answer
Self-consistency / best-of-N: sample multiple independent attempts, then vote or select
Verifier-guided search: explore a tree of reasoning steps, pruning weak branches early

slides.title: Three Strategies, Three Costs

rows: higher latency, more output tokens billed
pruned exploration of the reasoning tree

slides.title: The Same Model, Two Effort Settings
slides.body: Give a model a multi-step math word problem with an easy-to-miss unit conversion.
bullets: Low effort (single pass): the model locks into an early arithmetic slip and never revisits it
High effort: it drafts intermediate steps, notices the unit mismatch mid-reasoning, backtracks, and re-derives the answer
Same weights, same prompt — only the reasoning budget changed, and that changed the outcome
This is exactly the pattern behind "thinking effort" toggles shipping in current reasoning-model releases

slides.title: The Bill Comes Due at Inference
slides.body: Test-time compute is a real lever, but it's not a substitute for the model actually knowing something.
bullets: Simple factual lookups or short-form tasks get zero benefit from extra thinking — just added latency and cost
It cannot fix a model that fundamentally lacks the requisite knowledge; no amount of reasoning invents a fact it was never trained on
Production systems need a hard per-request budget, or costs become unpredictable under load
Some tasks are better served by a retrieval call or a tool call than by "thinking" longer

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Inference-time scaling is now a first-class lever alongside train-time scaling
Current model releases expose an explicit effort dial rather than one fixed reasoning depth
Match the strategy to the task: chain-of-thought for step-by-step problems, best-of-N when there's a cheap verifier, search when the branching factor is large
Always budget it — unbounded "thinking" is an unbounded bill

questions.prompt: What does "test-time compute" scaling mean?
options: Training on a larger test dataset
Spending more inference-time computation per query — longer reasoning, more samples, or search — instead of training a bigger model
Using a larger context window at inference
Caching previous answers to skip recomputation
questions.explanation: Test-time compute scaling trades training-time scale for inference-time scale: the same fixed model spends more computation per query via longer reasoning, multiple samples, or guided search.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the test-time compute strategies described?
options: Longer chain-of-thought reasoning
Self-consistency / best-of-N sampling
Quantizing the model's weights to int8
Verifier-guided search over reasoning steps
questions.explanation: Quantization reduces weight precision to save memory and speed up serving — it's a deployment-time technique, not a way of spending extra compute per query to improve accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why can't extra test-time compute fix every model failure?
options: It always makes latency worse than it helps accuracy
It can only reorganize what the model already knows, not supply knowledge it was never trained on
It only works for math problems
It requires retraining the model each time
questions.explanation: More reasoning steps or samples let a model explore and verify its own knowledge more thoroughly, but they can't inject facts or skills absent from training — that gap needs retrieval, tools, or retraining instead.

posts.title: Chinchilla Scaling Laws: How Much Data a Model Actually Needs
posts.subtitle: DeepMind proved most early LLMs were starved for data, not parameters
posts.summary: Chinchilla (DeepMind, 2022) showed that for a fixed compute budget, most LLMs were badly undertrained on data relative to their parameter count. Scaling model size and training tokens roughly together — not just piling on parameters — gets more accuracy per FLOP, which is why every serious lab now treats data volume as a first-class scaling lever.

slides.title: Bigger isn't always better — it's about the ratio
slides.body: For years, LLM progress meant one thing: more parameters. Chinchilla showed that was leaving performance on the table.

slides.title: Early LLMs were parameter-heavy, data-starved
slides.body: Before 2022, labs scaled model size aggressively but kept training data roughly fixed, assuming more weights always beat more tokens for a given compute budget.
bullets: GPT-3: 175B params, trained on ~300B tokens
Gopher (DeepMind, 2021): 280B params, also ~300B tokens
Same compute spent very differently on model vs. data was never tested rigorously

slides.title: The Chinchilla law: scale params and tokens together
slides.body: Hoffmann et al. (DeepMind, 2022) trained 400+ models at different size/data combinations under fixed compute budgets and fit a scaling law for the optimum.
bullets: Compute-optimal training needs model size (N) and training tokens (D) to grow at roughly the same rate
Rule of thumb that emerged: ~20 training tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training
Loss follows a predictable power law in N and D, letting you solve for the optimal split before spending compute

slides.title: Chinchilla (70B) beat Gopher (280B)
slides.body: Given the same training compute as Gopher, DeepMind trained a 4x smaller model on 4x more data — and it won.
bullets: Chinchilla: 70B params, 1.4T training tokens
Gopher: 280B params, ~300B training tokens — same compute budget as Chinchilla
Chinchilla outperformed Gopher, GPT-3, and Jurassic-1 across a broad benchmark suite despite being far smaller

slides.title: Params vs. tokens: the ratio matters
Why labs now deliberately break the rule
slides.body: Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute, not inference cost — and inference is what you pay for millions of times after release.
bullets: LLaMA (Meta, 2023) trained a 7B model on ~1T tokens — roughly 140 tokens/param, far past Chinchilla-optimal
A smaller model trained longer costs more upfront but is cheaper and faster to serve forever after
Chinchilla-optimal is the right target only when training compute, not serving cost, is the binding constraint

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Compute-optimal training scales parameters and data together, not parameters alone
~20 tokens per parameter is the Chinchilla-optimal rule of thumb for minimizing training compute
Modern frontier models intentionally 'overtrain' past that ratio to cut long-run inference cost
Any time you see a scaling claim, ask: optimal for what — training FLOPs, or total cost of ownership?

questions.prompt: What was Chinchilla's core finding about pre-2022 LLMs like GPT-3 and Gopher?
options: They used the wrong attention mechanism
They were undertrained on data relative to their parameter count
They had too few parameters for their data
They used too much compute overall
questions.explanation: Models like Gopher and GPT-3 trained huge parameter counts on comparatively little data (roughly 1 token per parameter or less). Chinchilla showed that for the same compute budget, a smaller model trained on proportionally more data performed better.

questions.prompt: What is the Chinchilla-optimal rule of thumb for training tokens per parameter?
options: ~1 token per parameter
~5 tokens per parameter
~20 tokens per parameter
~200 tokens per parameter
questions.explanation: Chinchilla's scaling law fit suggested roughly 20 training tokens for every model parameter minimizes loss for a fixed training compute budget — the ratio Chinchilla itself (70B params, 1.4T tokens) was trained near.

questions.prompt: Why do modern frontier labs often train models well past the Chinchilla-optimal ratio?
options: Chinchilla's math was later found to be wrong
More data always hurts model quality past a point
Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute, not the inference cost paid over the model's lifetime
Regulations require a minimum dataset size
questions.explanation: Chinchilla optimizes for training-time compute. A model served millions of times benefits from being smaller and cheaper to run, so labs like Meta trained smaller LLaMA models on far more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal to lower long-run inference cost, accepting a higher training bill.

posts.title: Quantization: Shrinking Model Weights Without Losing the Plot
posts.subtitle: Trading bits per weight for a model that actually fits on your GPU
posts.summary: Quantization rounds a model's weights down from 16-bit floats to 8-bit or 4-bit integers, cutting memory and speeding up inference because LLM serving is usually bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound. Modern methods like AWQ protect the small set of high-impact weights while compressing the rest hard, so a 70B model can go from needing a multi-GPU server to fitting on a single card.

slides.title: A 70B model doesn't need 140GB of memory
slides.body: Quantization cuts the precision of each weight, shrinking multi-hundred-gigabyte models to something that fits on a single GPU — often with almost no quality loss.

slides.title: Full precision is overkill for inference
slides.body: Models train in 16-bit floats, but shipping that same precision to production wastes memory bandwidth.
bullets: A 70B-parameter model at FP16 (2 bytes/weight) needs ~140GB just for weights, before activations or KV cache
LLM inference is usually memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound: every forward pass has to stream the full weight set through GPU memory
Weight distributions are narrow and models tolerate real rounding error — most of that precision isn't earning its keep at serving time

slides.title: Quantization: round weights to fewer bits
slides.body: Post-training quantization (PTQ) takes an already-trained model and compresses its weights directly, no retraining required.
bullets: INT8: 16-bit weights → 8-bit integers, roughly halving memory, often near-lossless with proper calibration
INT4: halves memory again (~4x smaller than FP16) — the sweet spot for running large models on a single consumer or workstation GPU, with a small but real quality hit
Not all weights matter equally: methods like AWQ scale and protect a small subset of high-magnitude "salient" weight channels at higher precision while quantizing the rest aggressively
Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the alternative: simulate low precision during fine-tuning so the model adapts to it, giving better accuracy at very low bit-widths than PTQ alone

slides.title: Worked example: fitting Llama-class 70B on one GPU
slides.body: The same 70B-parameter model at different precisions changes what hardware it needs entirely.
bullets: FP16: 70B × 2 bytes ≈ 140GB → needs multiple 80GB-class datacenter GPUs
INT8: ≈ 70GB → still needs two or more high-end GPUs
INT4 (GPTQ/AWQ, or GGUF Q4_K_M): ≈ 35-40GB → fits on a single 48GB card, or two consumer 24GB cards
Real tradeoff: 4-bit quantization of a 70B model typically costs a small, measurable amount of benchmark accuracy — often worth it to go from "needs a server" to "runs on a workstation"

slides.title: Precision vs. size vs. quality
slides.body: Lower bit-widths keep shrinking the model, but the quality cost grows non-linearly.

slides.title: Pitfall: aggregate benchmarks can hide real damage
slides.body: Quantization is lossy rounding, not compression — and its damage isn't evenly distributed.
bullets: Lower bit-widths hit some capabilities harder than others: multi-step reasoning and long-context coherence tend to degrade faster than simple pattern matching
A quantized model can score nearly identically on an average benchmark while failing badly on specific prompts — averages mask outlier regressions
When NOT to quantize aggressively: precision-sensitive tasks (medical, legal, code with subtle correctness bugs) where the last few points of accuracy matter most
Quantization is applied at inference time in almost all cases — training itself still happens in higher precision (BF16/FP16), with QAT as the exception when very low bit-widths are the target

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Quantization trades weight precision for memory and speed — near-lossless down to INT8, a real-but-often-acceptable hit at INT4
PTQ methods (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF-based tools) quantize an already-trained model in one pass; QAT bakes low precision into training for better low-bit accuracy
Not all weights matter equally — modern methods protect high-impact weight channels while compressing the rest harder
Always benchmark the quantized model on your actual task and spot-check real prompts, not just aggregate perplexity, before shipping

questions.prompt: Why is memory bandwidth usually the inference bottleneck for large LLMs, not raw compute?
options: GPUs cannot do floating point math fast enough for LLMs
Every forward pass must stream the full set of weights through memory, and that transfer often takes longer than the matrix multiplications themselves
Quantization has no effect on compute or memory
LLMs don't use matrix multiplication during inference
questions.explanation: Inference is typically memory-bound: generating each token requires streaming the model's weights through GPU memory. Shrinking weight size directly attacks that bottleneck, which is why quantization speeds up inference and not just memory footprint.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes AWQ from a naive "round every weight equally" approach?
options: AWQ retrains an entirely new model from scratch at low precision
AWQ identifies weights that matter most based on activation magnitude and preserves their precision while quantizing the rest more aggressively
AWQ only works for 8-bit quantization
AWQ removes weights entirely rather than reducing precision
questions.explanation: AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) observes that a small fraction of weight channels have outsized impact on outputs and protects those, preserving more quality than uniformly quantizing every weight the same way.

questions.prompt: A team quantizes a 70B model to INT4 and finds aggregate benchmark scores barely change. What should they still check?
options: Nothing further — an aggregate benchmark score fully guarantees reliability
Whether the model still runs on a GPU at all
Specific prompts and known failure modes, since low bit-widths can cause outlier errors on particular inputs even when averages hold up
The file size of the original FP16 checkpoint
questions.explanation: Aggregate benchmarks average across many examples and can mask outlier failures introduced by quantization. Spot-checking real prompts and known-hard cases catches regressions a single averaged metric hides.

posts.title: MCP Resources: Data a Server Exposes Without a Tool Call
posts.subtitle: The read-only, URI-addressed primitive that fills context before the model even asks
posts.summary: MCP Resources let a server expose data — files, database rows, logs — by URI, so a client can read it into context directly, without the model having to guess it should call a tool. Unlike Tools, which the model invokes, Resources are typically application-controlled: the host decides what actually gets attached.

slides.title: Not every piece of context needs a tool call
slides.body: MCP Resources let a server expose data by URI, so a client can pull it into context directly — without the round-trip of a model deciding to invoke a tool.

slides.title: Tools weren't built for exposing static data
slides.body: If a server only had Tools, surfacing a README or a table schema means the model must decide to call something first.
bullets: With only Tools, exposing "read this file" means the model has to decide to call a tool, wait for a result, then reason about it — extra latency and reasoning steps for what's often just static data
Some data belongs in context proactively (a project's README, an open ticket, a schema) rather than fetched on demand only if a model happens to guess it should ask
MCP splits "the model decides to act" (Tools) from "the application decides what's readable" (Resources) — two different control planes for two different jobs

slides.title: Resources: URI-addressed, read-only data
slides.body: Every resource is identified by a URI and described with metadata a client can browse before fetching.
bullets: Every resource has a URI (file:///, postgres://, https://, or a custom scheme the server defines), a name, optional description, and a mimeType
resources/list returns the fixed catalog of resources the server currently offers
resources/templates/list returns parameterized URI templates (RFC 6570) for resources the server can generate on demand — e.g. "file:///logs/{date}.log" instead of listing every log file
resources/read takes a URI and returns contents — each entry carries a uri, mimeType, and either text or a base64 blob for binary data
Resources are read-only by design: they describe what's available to read, not actions to take — that's what Tools are for

slides.title: Who decides what gets attached?
slides.body: Control is split deliberately between the model and the host application.
bullets: Tools are model-controlled: the model chooses when to call them based on the conversation

Resources are typically application-controlled: the host app (an IDE, a chat client) decides which resources to surface, often via a UI where a user picks "@file" or "+ attach", and the client then fetches and injects the content

This matters for cost and safety: a server can expose thousands of resources without the model ever seeing that full catalog by default, since the client — not the model — decides what actually gets read and injected

Servers can push notifications/resources/list_changed when the catalog changes, and support resources/subscribe so a client gets notifications/resources/updated when one specific resource's content changes

slides.title: Worked example: a database MCP server
slides.body: Resources make a table's schema visible without the model having to guess a query first.
bullets: resources/list returns each table as a resource, e.g. postgres://mydb/orders, mimeType application/json, description "Orders table schema + row count"
A user asks their coding assistant to look at the orders table; the client attaches that resource by calling resources/read and gets back the schema, injected straight into context
The client later calls resources/subscribe on that URI; if a migration adds a column, the server sends notifications/resources/updated so the client can re-read and keep context fresh
Contrast: if the server only exposed a query_database Tool, the model would have to guess correct SQL and issue a tool call just to see the schema — Resources skip that guesswork entirely

slides.title: Resources vs. Tools vs. Prompts
slides.body: MCP's three core primitives serve different purposes and are invoked by different parties.

slides.title: Pitfall: Resources aren't a guaranteed channel
slides.body: Whether a resource reaches the model depends entirely on the host application's support and UI.
bullets: If the client's UI never surfaces a resource, or the host doesn't implement the resources capability at all, that data simply never reaches the model — don't rely on Resources for anything the model absolutely must see

Large resources (a huge log file, a full table dump) can blow the context window if attached wholesale — scope them with templates or pagination instead of exposing "the whole database" as one resource
Not every client implements subscriptions or list-changed notifications — check a client's declared capabilities before depending on live updates
When to prefer a Tool instead: if the read needs a parameter the model decides mid-conversation ("search logs for X"), a Tool with a query argument fits more naturally than a static Resource

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Resources are MCP's read-only, URI-addressed primitive for exposing data — distinct from Tools (model-invoked actions) and Prompts (user-invoked templates)
Control typically sits with the application, not the model: the host decides what gets attached to context, keeping large resource catalogs from silently consuming model reasoning
resources/list (or resources/templates/list for parameterized ones) discovers what's available; resources/read fetches content; resources/subscribe plus notifications/resources/updated keep it fresh
Use Resources for data that should be readable on demand or attached explicitly; use Tools when the model needs to decide dynamically what to fetch or act on

questions.prompt: What's the key difference in "who decides" between MCP Tools and MCP Resources?
options: Tools are always free, Resources always cost tokens
The model decides when to call a Tool, while the host application typically decides which Resources get attached to context
Resources can only be used by the model, never by a human user
There's no functional difference — they're aliases for the same primitive
questions.explanation: MCP separates "the model acts" (Tools, model-controlled) from "the application curates" (Resources, typically application-controlled) — a client's UI usually decides what resource content actually reaches the model.

questions.prompt: How does a client discover parameterized resources a server can generate on demand, like a log file per date?
options: resources/list only, since templates aren't part of the spec
resources/templates/list, which returns RFC 6570 URI templates
By guessing valid URIs through trial and error
Only through a separate Tool call
questions.explanation: MCP defines resources/templates/list for exposing parameterized resources via URI templates (RFC 6570), letting a server describe a whole family of addressable resources without listing every instance individually.

questions.prompt: Why might exposing an entire database as a single MCP resource be a bad idea?
options: MCP resources can't contain JSON data
It risks blowing the context window if attached wholesale — better to scope with templates, per-table resources, or pagination
Databases can't be exposed as resources under the spec
It would violate the resources-are-read-only constraint
questions.explanation: A resource that returns unbounded data risks consuming the entire context window if a client attaches it. Scoping resources — per table, per date, paginated — keeps each read a manageable size.

posts.title: Tokenization: Why Models Can't Count the R's in Strawberry
posts.subtitle: Text becomes sub-word tokens before a model ever sees a letter
posts.summary: LLMs never read raw characters — text is split into sub-word tokens by a Byte-Pair Encoding vocabulary before it hits the model. That single design choice explains why models botch letter-counting and simple arithmetic, and why the same prompt costs 3-5x more tokens in some languages than in English.

slides.title: The model never sees the word "strawberry"
slides.body: It sees a short sequence of sub-word tokens — and that gap between characters and tokens explains some of the strangest LLM failures.

slides.title: Characters are too slow, whole words are too many
slides.body: A tokenizer has to pick a unit of text. Both extremes fail.
bullets: Character-level: sequences get 4-5x longer, exploding compute (attention is O(n²) in sequence length)
Word-level: English alone needs a 100,000+ word vocabulary, and it still breaks on typos, new words, and non-English scripts
The fix: sub-word units — common words stay whole, rare words split into reusable pieces

slides.title: Byte-Pair Encoding: merge the most frequent pair, repeat
slides.body: BPE builds its vocabulary bottom-up from a huge text corpus, before the model ever trains.
bullets: Start with every individual byte/character as a token
Count every adjacent pair in the corpus; merge the single most frequent pair into a new token
Repeat merging tens of thousands of times — each merge adds one token to the vocabulary
Stop once the vocabulary hits a target size (GPT-4: ~100k, Llama 3: ~128k, GPT-4o: ~200k)
Result: common words like "the" become one token; rare words like "tokenization" split into pieces like "token"+"ization"

slides.title: Worked example: why the model can't spell
slides.body: Run "strawberry" through a GPT-style tokenizer and it doesn't come out as 10 letters.
bullets: "strawberry" → tokens ["straw", "berry"] — the model's internal representation has 2 units, not 10 characters
To count the R's, the model must recall which letters live inside opaque token IDs it never explicitly decomposed — it's guessing from training patterns, not counting
Same root cause behind "9.11 > 9.9": digit sequences get split inconsistently ("9.11" might tokenize differently than "9.9"), and the model compares token patterns, not numeric value
Fix in practice: prompting the model to space out letters ("s-t-r-a-w...") or use code execution for arithmetic sidesteps the tokenizer entirely

slides.title: Tokenizers aren't interchangeable
slides.body: Vocabulary size and algorithm differ by model family, and it changes real inference cost.

slides.title: Pitfall: some languages pay a token tax
slides.body: BPE vocabularies are trained on corpora dominated by English, so non-Latin scripts split into far more pieces.
bullets: English text: roughly 1 token per 4 characters on average
Languages like Hindi, Thai, or Burmese can need 3-5x more tokens for the same sentence — higher API cost and less usable context window for the same content
"Glitch tokens": rare training-corpus artifacts (odd usernames, repeated strings) can get their own token, then behave unpredictably because the model saw them too rarely to learn them well

When NOT to worry about it: for short English prompts and everyday chat use, tokenization effects are invisible — this matters most at scale (cost) or at the edges (spelling, arithmetic, non-English UX)

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Tokenization is a fixed preprocessing step (BPE, trained once) — the model never chooses how text is split
Sub-word tokens balance vocabulary size against sequence length; that's why context limits are measured in tokens, not words or characters
Character-level tasks (spelling, letter-counting, precise arithmetic) are naturally hard for LLMs because the model's smallest unit usually isn't a character
Vocabulary size and non-English efficiency vary a lot by model — worth checking before estimating cost or context budget for a multilingual product

questions.prompt: Why doesn't pure character-level tokenization win despite avoiding sub-word oddities?
options: Characters can't represent Unicode text
It makes sequences 4-5x longer, which blows up compute since attention scales quadratically with sequence length
Character-level tokenizers can't be trained with BPE
It requires a larger vocabulary than word-level tokenization
questions.explanation: Character-level tokenization actually needs a *smaller* vocabulary, not larger — its cost is sequence length. Since self-attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, splitting text into individual characters multiplies compute for the same content.

questions.prompt: What does Byte-Pair Encoding do to build its vocabulary?
options: It randomly samples substrings from the training corpus
It asks a language model to propose useful word pieces
It repeatedly finds the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens in the corpus and merges it into a new token
It splits text on whitespace and punctuation only
questions.explanation: BPE starts from individual bytes/characters and greedily merges the most frequent adjacent pair at each step, growing the vocabulary one merge at a time until it hits the target size.

questions.prompt: Why do LLMs often struggle to compare numbers like 9.11 and 9.9 correctly?
options: They were never trained on any numeric data
Floating-point numbers are outside their vocabulary entirely
Digit sequences can be split into tokens inconsistently, so the model is pattern-matching token chunks rather than reasoning over numeric value
The comparison operator is ambiguous in natural language
questions.explanation: Because tokenization isn't guaranteed to split numbers digit-by-digit or consistently across values, the model ends up comparing dissimilar token sequences instead of true numeric magnitude — a direct side effect of sub-word tokenization, not a reasoning failure alone.

posts.title: Prime Agent: The Harness That Edits Its Own Playbook
posts.subtitle: Recursive subagent calls plus a self-editing memory push one benchmark from 30% to 95.5%.
posts.summary: Prime Agent is an open-source coding/research harness built on the Recursive Language Model abstraction: context as a variable, subagents as function calls, and a self-editing memory (the Continual Harness) that persists across sessions. On top of an unchanged Claude Opus 5, it reports pushing ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5% — a self-reported, not-yet-verified result worth reading with real skepticism.

slides.title: Prime Agent
bullets: Open-source coding & research harness from Prime Intellect + Princeton
Built on the Recursive Language Model (RLM) abstraction
Self-reported: ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 jumps from 30% to 95.5%

slides.title: Long-horizon work breaks single-shot agents
bullets: Most coding/research agents run one flat loop: read context, call a tool, repeat — with no durable memory between sessions.
Spin up a subagent to handle a subtask and its results vanish once it returns; nothing it learned carries forward.
Disconnect a terminal mid-task and the agent's state is gone — there's no daemon to reattach to.

slides.title: Treat context as a variable, subagents as function calls
slides.body: Prime Agent runs inside a persistent Python REPL. The Recursive Language Model (RLM) abstraction lets the model hold prompts as variables and call rlm(...) to spawn child agents programmatically — recursion instead of a fixed tool schema.
bullets: rlm(...) subagents run as real function calls inside the REPL, returning results the parent can immediately reuse in code.
Subagents can message each other directly — coordination doesn't have to round-trip through the top-level agent or the user.
The REPL itself is the tool: file edits, shell commands, and orchestration all happen as Python, not a rigid tool-call schema.

slides.title: The Continual Harness is memory that edits itself
slides.body: A /refine command reviews the current trajectory and writes small, evidence-backed updates to durable state — memories, skill descriptions, reusable subagent specs — that persist across sessions.
bullets: Sessions are daemon-backed: close the terminal, reattach later, and the agent's state and history are still there.
Refinements are incremental and evidence-backed, not wholesale rewrites — the harness edits what it learned, not what it assumes.
Turn, token, and time budgets plus quality gates keep the self-editing loop from running away unchecked.

slides.title: 95.5% on ARC-AGI-3 — with an asterisk
bullets: RHAE (Relative Human Action Efficiency) scores how few actions the agent needed relative to a human, with a squared penalty for inefficiency.
The 95.5% figure is self-reported by Prime Intellect and not yet on ARC's verified leaderboard — read it as directionally striking but unverified.
Same underlying model (Claude Opus 5) throughout; the harness, not the model, is what moved the number.

slides.title: A GPU-kernel task, worked through the harness
slides.body: Ask Prime Agent to write a faster CUDA kernel. It drafts an attempt in the REPL, spawns an rlm() subagent to benchmark it against a baseline, and gets back a failure trace.
bullets: On failure, /refine writes a note to the Continual Harness: check shared-memory bank conflicts before assuming occupancy is the bottleneck.
The next attempt — this session or a future one — starts with that note already in its skill library, so it doesn't repeat the same wrong hypothesis.
The same loop is reported to hold up on long-context coding, emulator construction, and autonomous nanoGPT training speedruns.

slides.title: Not a sandbox — and not a verified score
bullets: Prime Agent runs model-generated Python and shell commands with your user permissions; the project's own docs say explicitly it is 'not a security sandbox.'
Recursive rlm() calls multiply token and compute cost — every subagent is another model call, so budgets and quality gates matter as much as capability.
Skip it for short, single-turn tasks or anywhere untrusted code needs isolation; the self-editing harness is built for long-running, trusted work.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: RLM turns context into a variable and subagents into function calls — recursion replaces a fixed tool-call loop.
The Continual Harness is what makes it 'self-improving': small, evidence-backed edits to memory persist across sessions via /refine.
The 95.5% ARC-AGI-3 number is a self-reported harness result on an unchanged model — apply the same skepticism you'd give any unverified leaderboard entry.

questions.prompt: In the RLM abstraction, what does rlm(...) do inside Prime Agent's persistent REPL?
options: Spawns a recursive subagent as a normal function call, returning its result to the parent's code
Restarts the language model with a cleared context window
Compiles the current Python session into a fixed tool schema
Sends a webhook notification to the user's terminal
questions.explanation: RLM treats prompts as variables and subagents as callable functions — rlm(...) runs a child agent and hands its output straight back into the parent's running code, which is what lets subagents compose and coordinate.

questions.prompt: What does the Continual Harness's /refine command actually change?
options: The model's underlying weights, via a small fine-tuning step
Durable harness state — memories, skill descriptions, and subagent specs — through small, evidence-backed updates
The pricing tier of the API call
The ARC-AGI-3 benchmark's official leaderboard entry
questions.explanation: Prime Agent never touches model weights. /refine reviews the trajectory and edits durable, external state — the harness's own memory — so future sessions start smarter without any retraining.

questions.prompt: Why should the 95.5% ARC-AGI-3 RHAE score be read with caution?
options: It was measured on a much easier version of the benchmark
It's a self-reported result not yet on ARC's verified leaderboard, and it swaps out the harness, not the underlying model
The benchmark has since been deprecated
It only reflects performance on multiple-choice questions
questions.explanation: Prime Intellect reports the number themselves; ARC-AGI-3's official leaderboard still lists Opus 5 alone at 30.2%. The harness produced a large jump on the same model, but that jump hasn't been independently verified yet.

posts.title: A2A: The Protocol for Agents Talking to Agents
posts.subtitle: MCP wires a model to tools. A2A wires one agent to another.
posts.summary: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol, created by Google and now governed by the Linux Foundation, that standardizes how independent agents discover each other's capabilities and delegate work — the horizontal layer MCP was never built to cover. Agent Cards advertise capability, Tasks carry work through a real lifecycle, and Artifacts return structured results.

slides.title: A2A: Agent2Agent Protocol
bullets: An open protocol for agents built by different teams and vendors to discover and delegate work to each other
Created by Google, donated to the Linux Foundation in June 2025 with 100+ companies backing it
Complements MCP — MCP wires a model to tools, A2A wires one agent to another

slides.title: MCP solves the wrong half of the problem
bullets: MCP standardizes how one agent reaches tools, files, and data sources — a vertical connection between an app and its resources.
It says nothing about how two independent agents, each with their own model and tools behind a closed door, should talk to each other.
Before A2A, teams either hand-rolled a bespoke API per pair of agents, or forced every agent through the same framework — killing interoperability.

slides.title: Agent Cards: capability without exposing internals
slides.body: Every A2A-compliant agent publishes an Agent Card — a JSON manifest describing what it can do, how to reach it, and what auth it needs — without revealing its prompts, model, or tools.
bullets: A caller reads the card, decides if the agent fits the task, and never needs to know whether it's Claude, GPT, or a hand-built classifier underneath.
This is what makes agents 'opaque' by design: capability is discoverable, implementation stays private.
If a request doesn't match any local capability, an agent can route it to another agent whose card advertises a better fit.

slides.title: Tasks move through real states, not one request/response
slides.body: The unit of work in A2A is a Task, identified by an ID and tracked through a defined lifecycle — because agent work can take seconds or days.
bullets: submitted -> working -> completed / failed / canceled, plus input-required and auth-required for work that needs a human or credentials mid-flight.
Long-running tasks stream progress over Server-Sent Events (tasks/sendSubscribe), or push a webhook POST when the caller has disconnected.
Outputs come back as Artifacts built from Parts — text, file references, or structured data — not a single opaque blob.

slides.title: MCP and A2A operate at different layers
bullets: They're complementary, not competing: an A2A agent commonly uses MCP internally to reach its own tools before ever exposing a Task to another agent.

slides.title: Booking a trip across three agents
slides.body: A travel-planner agent gets 'book me a flight and hotel for the conference.' It doesn't own flight or hotel search — it delegates.
bullets: It reads the Agent Card of a flight-search agent, submits a Task with the trip constraints, and gets a task ID back immediately.
While that task is 'working,' it submits a second Task to a hotel-search agent in parallel — both run independently, each streaming status over SSE.
When a fare requires a login the planner doesn't have, the flight agent flips the task to 'input-required' instead of failing outright, and the planner relays that back to the user.

slides.title: Skip it for anything that fits in one process
bullets: If one team owns both sides and the call is a single synchronous request, plain function calling or MCP is simpler — A2A's task lifecycle is overhead you don't need.
A public Agent Card and a webhook endpoint are both attack surface: verify who's calling before you execute a delegated Task, and treat card claims as untrusted until an agent proves them.
Cross-agent debugging is harder — a failure three delegated Tasks deep means tracing state across services you don't own, not just reading one stack trace.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A2A standardizes agent-to-agent delegation the way MCP standardized agent-to-tool access — the two are meant to stack, not substitute.
Agent Cards make capability discoverable while keeping an agent's internals opaque; Tasks give delegated work a real lifecycle instead of one blocking call.
Reach for it when agents cross team or vendor boundaries and work can run long; skip it inside a single process where a normal function call already does the job.

questions.prompt: What problem does A2A solve that MCP does not?
options: How a model calls a single tool synchronously
How two independent agents, possibly from different vendors, discover each other's capabilities and delegate work
How to fine-tune a model on new data
How to cache repeated prompts to cut token cost
questions.explanation: MCP wires an agent to tools and data (a vertical connection). A2A wires one agent to another (a horizontal connection) — the layer MCP was never designed to cover.

questions.prompt: What is an Agent Card?
options: A trading card generated for viral marketing
A JSON manifest an agent publishes describing its capabilities and how to reach it, without exposing its internals
A log of every Task an agent has completed
A billing record for API usage
questions.explanation: The Agent Card is how A2A keeps agents 'opaque': callers can evaluate whether an agent fits a task from its published capabilities alone, without seeing its prompts, model, or tools.

questions.prompt: A Task assigned 'input-required' status in A2A means:
options: The task failed permanently and must be resubmitted from scratch
The task needs additional information or human input before it can continue
The requesting agent's authentication has expired
The task completed successfully with a partial artifact
questions.explanation: A2A's task lifecycle includes states built for real-world friction — input-required and auth-required let a task pause for a missing piece rather than failing outright.

posts.title: MCP Sampling: The Server Calls Back to the Model
posts.subtitle: Tools let the model call the server. Sampling lets the server call the model.
posts.summary: Sampling is the MCP primitive that flips the usual direction: instead of the model calling a server tool, the server asks the client to run a completion for it, with the human able to inspect or veto every request. It lets thin, credential-free servers borrow real reasoning without ever holding an API key.

slides.title: The One MCP Primitive That Runs Backwards
slides.body: Tools, Resources, and Prompts all flow one way: client and model reach into the server. Sampling reverses it — the server reaches into the model.

slides.title: A server sometimes needs to think, not just fetch
slides.body: Imagine an MCP server that watches a huge log stream or a big diff. It could return the raw data and let the orchestrating model make sense of it — but that can blow the context budget, and a naive filter can't judge nuance the way a language model can.
bullets: Returning everything wastes context tokens on noise
A hand-written heuristic can't judge severity or intent
The server would need its own LLM API key to reason locally — a credential most servers shouldn't hold

slides.title: sampling/createMessage: the server borrows the client's model
slides.body: MCP defines a request the SERVER sends to the CLIENT: sampling/createMessage. The client — which already holds the model connection and the user's trust — runs the completion and hands the text back to the server.
bullets: Server never touches an API key or model credential
Client decides which actual model serves the request; the server only sends optional 'modelPreferences' hints (intelligence vs. speed priority)
The completion is scoped to exactly the messages the server includes — not the user's full conversation

slides.title: Human-in-the-loop is mandatory, not optional
slides.body: The spec requires the client to give the user visibility into a sampling request before it runs, and again before the result goes back to the server.
bullets: Client SHOULD show the user the proposed prompt and let them edit or reject it
Client SHOULD show the completion before releasing it to the server
This is what makes it safe for a server to 'use AI' without becoming a second, unaudited gatekeeper of the model

slides.title: Sampling vs. the other three MCP primitives
Worked example: a diff-review server
slides.body: A code-review MCP server pulls a 4,000-line diff from a webhook. Instead of dumping it into the calling agent's context, it uses sampling to pre-digest it.
bullets: Server sends sampling/createMessage with the diff and a prompt: 'flag risky changes only'
Client's model (chosen by the client, not the server) reads the diff and returns a 200-word risk summary
Server returns just that summary as the tool result — the orchestrating agent's context never sees the raw diff
Net effect: one extra model round-trip buys a large reduction in tokens spent downstream

slides.title: Where it breaks, and what to remember
slides.body: Sampling is powerful but easy to misuse.
bullets: It's an OPTIONAL client capability — many MCP clients don't implement it yet, so servers must degrade gracefully if it's absent
A server that fires sampling requests in a loop can rack up real model cost and latency behind the user's back — rate-limit it server-side
Approval prompts add friction; reserve sampling for steps that genuinely need judgment, not every server action
Remember the core inversion: Tools are the model reaching OUT to the server; Sampling is the server reaching BACK into the model

questions.prompt: In MCP, which direction does a sampling/createMessage request travel?
options: From the model to the server, like a tool call
From the server to the client, asking it to run a completion
From the user directly to the model, bypassing the server
From one server to another server
questions.explanation: Sampling reverses the usual flow: the SERVER sends the request, and the CLIENT (which owns the model connection) executes it and returns the completion — the only MCP primitive that lets a server 'use AI' without holding its own model credentials.

questions.prompt: Why does the MCP spec require human-in-the-loop review for sampling requests?
options: To make responses slower for security theater
Because servers are not allowed to see any model output
Because a server could otherwise trigger model completions the user never sees or approves, using the user's model access
It doesn't — sampling is fully automatic by design
questions.explanation: Since the server never holds its own API key, sampling effectively lets it spend the user's model access. Requiring the client to surface the prompt and result for approval keeps that spend and content visible to the human instead of happening silently.

questions.prompt: A server needs to summarize a huge log file before returning results to the orchestrating agent, to avoid blowing its context budget. Which MCP primitive fits best?
options: Resources, because logs are just static context
Prompts, because summarization is a template
Sampling, so the server can get a model-generated summary before responding
Tools, because the server should expose the raw log as a tool result
questions.explanation: This is exactly the sampling use case: the server needs judgment (what's worth keeping) that a fixed template or raw dump can't provide, so it asks the client to run a completion and returns the condensed result instead of the raw data.

posts.title: ReAct: Reasoning and Acting in the Same Loop
posts.subtitle: A written thought before every tool call — the pattern that turned LLMs from answerers into agents.
posts.summary: ReAct interleaves a short written thought with every tool call and its resulting observation, so an agent reasons about what it just learned before deciding what to do next. It's a prompting pattern, not an architecture change, and it's the scaffold underneath most 'agentic' LLM products today.

slides.title: Think, Then Act, Then Look
slides.body: ReAct interleaves a written thought with every tool call and every observation, so an agent reasons about what it just learned before deciding what to do next.
bullets: Introduced by Yao et al. in 2022 as 'ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models'
The scaffold underneath most 'agentic' LLM products today, from research assistants to coding agents
Not a new architecture — a prompting structure: Thought, Action, Observation, repeat

slides.title: Pure Reasoning Hallucinates, Pure Acting Has No Plan
slides.body: Before ReAct, agent designs mostly fell into two camps, each missing half the picture.
bullets: Chain-of-thought prompting reasons step by step but never touches the outside world — an early wrong guess compounds silently, with nothing to catch it
Naive 'action-only' agents call tools and act on whatever comes back, with no explicit deliberation about whether the last result actually helped
Neither camp lets reasoning and evidence correct each other mid-task

slides.title: Thought, Action, Observation — Repeat
slides.body: ReAct threads a short natural-language thought before each action, and feeds the tool's real result back in as an observation the next thought can react to.
bullets: Thought: the model writes a sentence of reasoning about the current state and what to do next
Action: it emits a tool call (search, lookup, code execution) chosen based on that thought
Observation: the tool's real output is appended to the context, verbatim
The loop repeats until a Thought concludes with a Finish[answer] action

slides.title: Built With Prompting, Not New Weights
slides.body: The original ReAct paper implements the whole pattern with few-shot exemplars in the prompt — no architecture change and no extra training required to get it working.
bullets: A handful of hand-written Thought/Action/Observation traces go in the prompt as examples
The harness parses each model turn: if it's an Action, execute the tool and inject the Observation; if it's Finish, stop and return the answer
Later systems fine-tune models directly on ReAct-style traces so the format doesn't rely on few-shot examples at all
This is the same act-observe scaffold most native tool-calling APIs now bake in directly

slides.title: Answering a Question That Needs Two Lookups
slides.body: A worked trace for: 'Which city is home to the headquarters of the company that makes the iPhone?'
bullets: Thought 1: 'I need the iPhone's manufacturer before I can find a headquarters.' Action: Search[iPhone manufacturer]. Observation: Apple Inc.
Thought 2: 'Now I need Apple's headquarters city.' Action: Search[Apple Inc. headquarters]. Observation: Cupertino, California.
Thought 3: 'I have both facts chained together, I can answer now.' Action: Finish[Cupertino, California]
Each thought picks the next query using only what's been observed so far — not a fixed plan written up front

slides.title: ReAct vs. Chain-of-Thought-Only vs. Act-Only
slides.body: On the multi-step QA and interactive decision-making benchmarks in the original paper, ReAct's traces were far more interpretable than either baseline, since every action arrived with a stated reason attached.

rows: No — reasons purely from the model's own memory
Confidently wrong on facts outside training data
Yes — but with no deliberation between calls
Wastes calls or misreads a result with nothing correcting course
Yes — every action is chosen by a preceding thought
Can still loop or misread an observation, but errors show up in the trace

slides.title: Where ReAct Falls Down
bullets: Thought-action loops can repeat: the model re-issues a similar search after a bad observation instead of trying a different angle
Every thought is extra tokens and extra latency — for a single factual lookup, one tool call beats a multi-turn ReAct loop
A wrong observation (a bad search result, a stale API response) gets reasoned over as if it were true — ReAct doesn't verify evidence, it just reacts to it
Needs either good few-shot exemplars or fine-tuning on traces; a model with weak instruction-following can drift out of the format entirely

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: ReAct = write a thought before every action, feed the real observation back in, repeat until Finish
It's a prompting/scaffolding pattern, not a model architecture — buildable with few-shot examples or fine-tuning
It beats pure chain-of-thought (no grounding) and pure act-only (no deliberation) by letting reasoning and evidence correct each other mid-task
Skip it for single-lookup tasks, where the extra thought steps just add latency without changing the outcome

questions.prompt: In the ReAct loop, what does the 'Observation' step contain?
options: The model's next planned action
The real, verbatim result returned by the tool the action just called
A critique of the previous thought
A summary of the entire conversation so far
questions.explanation: Observation is the actual output of whatever tool or action was just executed — search results, an API response, code output — injected back into context so the next Thought can reason over real evidence, not a guess.

questions.prompt: Why does ReAct tend to hallucinate less than pure chain-of-thought prompting on knowledge-heavy questions?
options: It always uses a larger model
Its thoughts are grounded by real tool observations instead of reasoning purely from the model's parametric memory
It skips reasoning entirely and only acts
It requires beam search decoding
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought alone reasons from what the model already 'knows' internally, so an early wrong guess compounds silently. ReAct's thoughts are checked against real observations pulled from tools, giving the model a chance to correct course mid-task.

questions.prompt: What's a realistic failure mode of a ReAct agent?
options: It cannot call external tools at all
It re-issues a similar unhelpful action after a bad observation instead of changing its approach
It always terminates after exactly one step
It requires no prompt engineering whatsoever
questions.explanation: Because each thought reasons mainly over the immediate observation, a ReAct agent can get stuck repeating a similar query when the tool keeps returning unhelpful results, instead of stepping back to try a fundamentally different action.
