posts.title: Prompt Caching: Skipping the Prefill You've Already Paid For
posts.subtitle: Same system prompt, same tools, same 5,000 tokens — why recompute it on every call?
posts.summary: Prompt caching lets an LLM API skip re-running the expensive prefill pass over a prompt prefix it has already processed, by persisting that prefix's KV cache between calls instead of just within one generation. It only works on an exact, token-for-token prefix match, so cache hit rate depends entirely on putting static content (system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples) before anything that varies from call to call. It's a huge win for agents and chat apps that reuse a large shared prefix across many requests, but a single early-token change — even a timestamp — silently blows the whole cache away.

slides.title: Stop Re-Reading the Same Prefix Every Call
slides.body: Prompt caching persists the KV cache for a shared prompt prefix across separate API calls, so a long system prompt or tool schema gets prefilled once and reused, not recomputed on every request.

slides.title: Every Call Re-Prefills the Same Tokens
slides.body: An LLM has to run a full forward pass over every input token before it can generate the first output token — that's prefill, and it happens fresh on each API call unless something intervenes.
bullets: An agent with a 5,000-token system prompt plus tool definitions pays that same prefill cost on call 1, call 2, ... call 50 of a session, even though the prefix never changed
Prefill scales with input length, so a long shared prefix dominates both latency (time-to-first-token) and cost on short-answer workloads
The regular KV cache only helps within a single generation — it's discarded the moment the response finishes and the connection closes
For RAG and agent apps, the shared prefix (instructions, tool schemas, retrieved docs) is often far longer than the part that actually changes per call

slides.title: Cache the Prefix's KV State, Not Just the Request
slides.body: Prompt caching persists the attention keys and values computed for a prompt prefix in provider-side memory for a short window, keyed off an exact match of the token sequence.
bullets: On a cache hit, the model skips recomputing attention for every cached token and starts decoding from where the cached prefix ends — only the new suffix tokens get prefilled
Matching is exact and positional: token 1 through token N of the new request must be byte-identical to the cached prefix, or the match breaks at the first divergence
Cached entries typically live for a short TTL (minutes, sometimes extendable to an hour) since providers can't hold every customer's KV state indefinitely
This is a provider-side optimization, not a model behavior change — the output is identical to running without caching, only the compute path differs

slides.title: Prefix Order Decides the Hit Rate
slides.body: Because the match is positional, everything that stays constant across calls has to come first in the prompt, and everything that varies has to come last.
bullets: Correct order: system prompt -> tool/function definitions -> few-shot examples -> (cache boundary) -> retrieved context or conversation history that changes per call -> the new user turn
Put a timestamp, a random request id, or even reordered JSON keys anywhere before the cache boundary and every later request misses the cache, since the prefix no longer matches token-for-token
Some APIs require an explicit cache breakpoint marker in the request; others cache automatically once a prefix crosses a minimum token threshold
Multi-turn chat naturally grows a cacheable prefix: turn 3's prompt is turn 2's prompt plus new tokens, so each turn can hit the cache built by the previous one

slides.title: A Support Agent Across 40 Turns
slides.body: A customer-support agent ships a 3,000-token system prompt plus 2,000 tokens of tool schemas — a 5,000-token fixed prefix — in front of every call in a session.
bullets: Call 1: no cache exists yet, so all 5,000 prefix tokens plus the user's question get prefilled at full cost — this is the cache write
Calls 2 through 40: the 5,000-token prefix hits the cache and is skipped entirely; only the growing conversation tail and new user turn get prefilled fresh
Net effect over the session: roughly 200,000 prefix tokens worth of redundant computation across 40 calls collapses down to being paid for essentially once
If the app instead prepended a per-call random session id before the system prompt, every single one of those 40 calls would miss and re-pay full prefill cost

slides.title: Prompt Caching vs. Semantic Caching vs. In-Request KV Cache

rows: Embedding-similarity match on the whole query
Not really a 'cache' — reused only within one generation
Persists across separate API calls (minutes-scale TTL)
Persists across calls, often much longer TTL
Discarded the instant the response completes
Saves prefill compute; output is unchanged
Skips the LLM call entirely and returns a stored answer
Avoids recomputing attention for already-generated tokens
Built into every inference engine by default

slides.title: Where It Breaks: Ordering, TTL, and One-Off Calls
slides.body: Prompt caching is close to free to adopt, but it fails silently rather than throwing an error, which makes the failure mode easy to miss.
bullets: Dynamic content before the cache boundary (a date, a request id, reordered fields) invalidates the cache with no warning — you just quietly stop getting the discount and speed-up
Short TTLs mean a session that goes idle for too long between calls loses its cached prefix and pays full prefill again on the next request
One-off, single-call use cases get zero benefit: the very first call on any prefix is always a full-cost cache write, so caching only pays off when a prefix is reused multiple times
Very short prefixes usually fall below the minimum token threshold providers require before caching kicks in at all, so caching a tiny system prompt is often not worth the added complexity

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Prompt caching reuses the KV state of an exact-match prompt prefix across separate API calls, cutting prefill cost and time-to-first-token on repeated requests
Ordering is the whole game: static content (system prompt, tools, few-shot examples) first, variable content last, right up against the cache boundary
It only pays off when the same prefix is reused multiple times before its TTL expires — one-off calls always eat the full cache-write cost
A single token changed early in the prompt breaks the match silently — no error, just a quiet loss of the speed and cost benefit

questions.prompt: What has to be true for a new request to hit an existing prompt cache?
options: The new request must be semantically similar to a past request
The new request's prefix must be an exact, token-for-token match to the cached prefix
The new request must use a shorter system prompt than before
The model must be running on the same GPU as the original request
questions.explanation: Prompt caching matching is positional and exact — token 1 through N must be identical to what's cached. Unlike semantic caching, similarity doesn't count; any divergence at or before a given token breaks the match from that point on.

questions.prompt: An agent puts a fresh request-id string right after the system prompt but before the tool definitions. What happens to its prompt cache hit rate?
options: No effect, since request ids are ignored by the cache
It improves, because unique ids help the provider distinguish sessions
It collapses toward zero, because every call now has a different token sequence at that position, breaking the match for everything after it
The cache TTL automatically extends to compensate
questions.explanation: Because matching is positional, inserting anything variable before the tool definitions means the tool definitions (and everything after them) no longer sit at a matching prefix position across calls — the cache effectively never hits past that point.

questions.prompt: Why does prompt caching provide no benefit on a true one-off API call?
options: One-off calls are billed at a flat rate regardless of caching
The very first call on any prefix is always a full-price cache write — the savings only appear on later calls that reuse that same prefix
Prompt caching is disabled for calls without conversation history
One-off calls never contain a long enough prefix to qualify
questions.explanation: Caching has no history to reuse on the first call — that call pays full prefill cost while writing the cache. The discount and latency win only show up on subsequent calls that hit the prefix that was just written, so reuse is what makes it worthwhile.

posts.title: Continuous Batching: How LLM Servers Pack GPUs Full
posts.subtitle: The GPU slot doesn't wait for the slowest sequence in the batch to finish
posts.summary: Static batching groups requests together and runs the whole group until every sequence finishes, so a batch slot sits idle the moment its short reply is done but the batch's longest reply is still generating. Continuous (iteration-level) batching re-evaluates the batch after every single decoding step instead, evicting finished sequences and slotting in new requests immediately, so the GPU is never paying for idle slots. It pairs naturally with paged KV cache allocation, since batch membership keeps changing, but it isn't free: it needs real per-step scheduling logic and gives little benefit at very low, bursty request rates.

slides.title: One Slot, Many Requests, Zero Idle Time
slides.body: Continuous batching keeps every GPU batch slot working by re-deciding, at every decoding step, which requests belong in the batch — instead of locking the group in place until all of them finish.

slides.title: Static Batching Wastes the Fastest Requests
slides.body: A traditional batch scheduler groups requests together and keeps that group fixed until every sequence in it finishes generating.
bullets: If a batch pairs a 20-token reply with a 500-token reply, the 20-token one sits done in memory for the remaining 480 steps — occupying a slot but doing zero useful work
GPU utilization drops every time a sequence finishes early inside a still-running batch
New requests queue outside the batch entirely until the whole group completes, adding latency even when spare GPU capacity exists
Worst case: one unusually long generation blocks a whole batch of otherwise-fast requests from ever completing sooner

slides.title: Schedule Per Token, Not Per Batch
slides.body: Continuous batching — also called iteration-level scheduling — checks the batch's composition after every single decoding step, not once per full generation.
bullets: A finished sequence is evicted the instant it hits its stop condition, freeing its slot immediately
A queued request can start generating within one decode step of arriving, without waiting for the current batch to fully drain
The set of sequences being decoded together can be different at step 50 than it was at step 49
This idea was popularized by the Orca LLM serving system and is now standard in production inference engines

slides.title: Prefill and Decode Share the Same Loop
slides.body: A new request's prefill (processing its prompt into an initial KV cache) can be interleaved with the decode steps of sequences that are already generating, all inside the same batched matrix multiply.
bullets: Each request keeps its own KV cache, position ids, and stop condition even though many requests share one batched GPU call
Swapping sequences in and out cheaply requires a non-contiguous, page-table-style KV cache allocator (as in PagedAttention) — resizing one giant contiguous buffer every step would be far too slow
Production engines like vLLM, Hugging Face TGI, and TensorRT-LLM all implement some form of this per-step scheduling loop

slides.title: Static vs. Continuous Batching

rows: New request waits for the whole batch to finish
New request can join on the next decode step
GPU idles on any slot whose sequence finished early
A finished sequence's slot is reused immediately
Simple to implement; fixed, predictable memory layout
Needs per-step scheduling plus a paged KV cache allocator
Throughput bounded by the batch's longest sequence
Throughput bounded by aggregate GPU capacity, not one outlier

slides.title: Three Requests, One Living Batch
slides.body: Step 0: request A (expects ~300 tokens) and request B (expects ~20 tokens) start decoding together. By step 20, B hits its stop token and is evicted. Request C, which had been queued since step 12, is slotted into B's freed spot at step 21 and is already on its own 9th decode step by the time A finishes at step 300 — C never sat in an external queue waiting for A and B to both complete.
bullets: B occupies a batch slot for only its own 20 steps, not for all 300 steps that A needs
C starts generating one iteration after arriving, not after the entire original batch drains
The effective batch size can grow or shrink mid-generation as slots free up or new requests arrive

slides.title: When Continuous Batching Doesn't Pay Off
slides.body: The per-step scheduling and paged-memory machinery are real engineering cost, and they aren't free lunch for every workload.
bullets: At very low, bursty request rates (effective batch size near 1), there's nothing to interleave — the benefit shrinks toward zero
Without an explicit scheduling policy, a flood of long requests can still starve short ones of scheduler attention, even though slots are being reused
Per-step batch-composition checks add real scheduling overhead; naive implementations can introduce latency jitter under heavy, mixed-length load
It requires a non-contiguous KV cache manager — a meaningfully more complex serving stack than a fixed-shape static batch

slides.title: The Batch Is a Living Queue, Not a Fixed Group
bullets: Static batching wastes GPU cycles on slots held by sequences that already finished
Continuous batching re-evaluates batch membership after every decoding step
It pairs naturally with paged KV cache allocation (PagedAttention) for cheap slot swapping
It's overhead-heavy for low, bursty traffic, but it's what nearly every production LLM server (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM) uses under real concurrent load

questions.prompt: What triggers a batch-composition decision in continuous batching?
options: Every decoding step
Only when a new request arrives
Only when the batch is completely full
Once per minute, on a fixed timer
questions.explanation: Continuous batching re-checks which requests belong in the batch after every single decode step. That's what lets a finished sequence's slot get reused almost instantly instead of waiting for the whole batch to drain.

questions.prompt: In static batching, why does the GPU end up doing wasted work?
options: The model architecture is too small for the batch size
A sequence that finishes early still occupies its batch slot until every sequence in the group completes
Prefill is skipped entirely in static batching
The KV cache is deleted before decoding starts
questions.explanation: A short reply inside a static batch finishes generating but keeps its slot allocated until the longest sequence in that same batch also finishes — so the GPU produces no useful output on that slot for all the remaining steps.

questions.prompt: Why does continuous batching typically depend on a paged (non-contiguous) KV cache allocator?
options: It reduces the model's numerical precision
Batch membership changes every step, so sequences need to be added and removed cheaply without resizing one giant contiguous buffer each time
It removes the need to compute attention scores
It compresses the model's weight matrices on disk
questions.explanation: Because the batch's membership can change on every decode step, the KV cache allocator needs to add and evict sequences fast. Page-table-style block allocation (as in PagedAttention) makes that cheap; a single contiguous buffer would need expensive resizing or copying on every swap.

posts.title: Knowledge Distillation: Teaching a Small Model to Mimic a Big One
posts.subtitle: The teacher's wrong answers carry more signal than its right ones
posts.summary: Knowledge distillation trains a small 'student' model to reproduce a large 'teacher' model's full output distribution, not just its final answer — because the relative probabilities the teacher assigns to wrong answers ('dark knowledge') encode how it generalizes. A temperature-raised softmax exposes that structure, a KL-divergence loss transfers it, and the result is a compact model that captures far more of the teacher's behavior than training the same small architecture from scratch on hard labels ever could. It's not free: the student is capped by its own capacity, needs teacher inference during training, and can inherit the teacher's blind spots — so it's a targeted efficiency tool, not a universal fix.

slides.title: The Best Teacher Doesn't Just Give the Right Answer
slides.body: A large model asked to classify a handwritten '2' might output 0.7 for '2', 0.2 for '3', and 0.099 spread across everything else. That 0.2 isn't noise — it's the teacher telling you a '2' looks a bit like a '3'. Knowledge distillation trains a small model on that whole distribution, not just the label '2'.

slides.title: A Small Model Trained From Scratch Learns Less Than It Could
bullets: You often can't ship the giant model: a 70B-parameter LLM is too slow and too expensive for a latency-sensitive product surface, but a 7B model trained the normal way — on the same hard labels or the same next-token targets — usually falls well short of the big model's behavior.
Hard labels are a single one-hot vector: 'this token is X, everything else is 0.' That throws away all the information in how confident the model was, and which wrong answers it considered plausible.

The small model has to rediscover every pattern the large model learned, from the same finite training set, with far less capacity — it's learning from scratch what the teacher already learned from a much bigger training run.
The core question distillation answers: instead of making the student re-derive the teacher's knowledge, can you just transfer it directly?

slides.title: Train the Student to Match the Teacher's Full Distribution
bullets: The classic recipe (Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, 'Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network', 2015): run the teacher on the training data, keep its output probability distribution (the 'soft targets') instead of just the top prediction, and train the student to match that distribution with a KL-divergence loss.

In practice the student is trained on a blend: a distillation loss against the teacher's soft targets, plus (often) the normal loss against the real hard labels — a weighted mix rather than either alone.

For LLMs specifically, the 'label' at each position is a token, and the teacher's soft target is its full next-token probability distribution — so distillation transfers not just what the teacher would say, but how uncertain it was between alternatives, token by token.
This works with the student and teacher having completely different architectures or sizes — distillation only needs matching output spaces (the same vocabulary or class set), not matching internals.

slides.title: Temperature Is the Knob That Exposes 'Dark Knowledge'
bullets: A normal softmax at low temperature is spiky: one class near 1.0, everything else near 0 — that near-zero tail is where the useful similarity information lives, and it's too small to learn from as-is.

Raising the softmax temperature T (dividing logits by T before the softmax) flattens the distribution, pulling those near-zero probabilities up into a range the student can actually learn from — the same trick used to make a probability distribution 'softer' for sampling.

Hinton's term for this signal is 'dark knowledge': the teacher's relative ranking of wrong answers (a '2' looking more like a '3' than a '7') reflects learned structure in the input space that hard labels never expose.
Both teacher and student use the same raised temperature during distillation training, then the student is switched back to normal temperature (T=1) at inference time.

slides.title: Worked Example: Why the '2' vs '3' Signal Matters
slides.body: Two training images both labeled '2': one is written cleanly, the other has an open loop that could pass for a '3'.
bullets: Training on hard labels alone, both images produce the identical target: 100% '2', 0% everything else — the student gets no signal that the second image is a harder, more ambiguous case.

The teacher's soft output on the ambiguous image might be 65% '2', 30% '3', 5% other — training the student against that distribution teaches it exactly where the decision boundary between '2' and '3' is blurry.

Multiply this across an entire dataset: every example now carries a graded, per-class similarity signal instead of one bit of information, which is why a distilled student can match a from-scratch model of the same size trained on far more labeled data.
The same idea scales to LLMs: distilling next-token distributions teaches a small model which alternative phrasings or tokens the teacher considered close calls, not just which one it picked.

slides.title: Distillation vs. Pruning vs. Quantization

rows: Shrinking parameter count while keeping behavior
Removes weights/heads from the same model
Cutting size with minimal architecture change
Cutting memory/compute with the same architecture

slides.title: Where Distillation Falls Short
bullets: Capacity ceiling: a student can't exceed what its own architecture can represent — distillation transfers knowledge efficiently, but it can't make a 1B model 'contain' everything a 70B model knows.

Training cost isn't free: you need teacher inference over the whole training set (or on-the-fly during training), which for a huge teacher can be a significant compute cost of its own, on top of training the student.

Inherited blind spots: the student is optimized to match the teacher, including the teacher's systematic errors, biases, and hallucination patterns — distillation compresses behavior, it doesn't correct it.

Diminishing returns at extreme compression ratios: distilling a huge teacher into a very small student tends to transfer surface-level patterns well but loses the teacher's rarer, long-tail capabilities first.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Distillation trains a small student to match a large teacher's full output distribution, not just its top answer — the 'dark knowledge' in the near-zero probabilities is the whole point.
Temperature-scaled softmax is the mechanism that makes that dark knowledge learnable; the student typically trains against a blend of the teacher's soft targets and the real hard labels.
It composes with pruning and quantization rather than replacing them — the three techniques change different things (architecture, weight count, numeric precision).
It's an efficiency tool with real limits: a student is capped by its own capacity, costs teacher inference to produce, and inherits the teacher's errors along with its knowledge.

questions.prompt: In knowledge distillation, what is the student model primarily trained to match?
options: The teacher's single top-predicted label only
The teacher's full output probability distribution across all classes/tokens
The teacher's internal weight values layer by layer
The teacher's training dataset, resampled at random
questions.explanation: The whole point of distillation is the 'soft targets' — the teacher's full distribution over outputs, including the low probabilities it assigns to wrong answers. Those near-zero values ('dark knowledge') encode how the teacher generalizes, which a single hard label discards.

questions.prompt: What does raising the softmax temperature during distillation accomplish?
options: It makes the teacher's predictions more confident and spiky
It flattens the output distribution, making the small probabilities on wrong classes large enough to learn from
It reduces the number of parameters in the student model
It converts the teacher's outputs into hard one-hot labels
questions.explanation: A low-temperature softmax is spiky — one class near 1.0, the rest near 0. Dividing logits by a temperature T > 1 before the softmax spreads probability mass out, surfacing the relative differences between wrong answers so the student has a learnable signal instead of near-zero noise.

questions.prompt: Which limitation is specific to knowledge distillation, as opposed to quantization?
options: It cannot reduce inference latency at all
It requires running the teacher model to produce training targets, adding compute cost before the student is even trained
It only works on convolutional neural networks
It always requires the student and teacher to share identical architectures
questions.explanation: Quantization just reduces numeric precision on existing weights — no separate model needs to run. Distillation requires generating soft targets from the teacher (often over the whole training set), which is a real compute cost on top of training the student, and the student is still capped by its own capacity.

posts.title: FlashAttention: Rewriting Attention Around the Memory Wall
posts.subtitle: The bottleneck was never the math — it was moving data between GPU memory tiers
posts.summary: Standard self-attention is compute-quadratic, but on modern GPUs the real bottleneck is memory bandwidth: the naive kernel repeatedly writes and reads the full N×N attention matrix to slow HBM. FlashAttention fuses the matmul-softmax-matmul sequence into one kernel that tiles Q/K/V into fast on-chip SRAM and uses an online softmax trick, so it computes mathematically exact attention while never materializing that full matrix — turning quadratic memory into linear memory and delivering roughly a 2-4x training speedup in the original paper. It's an IO-aware systems rewrite, not an approximation, which is why it composes with quantization, GQA, and paged KV caches rather than replacing them.

slides.title: Attention's Bottleneck Was Never the Math
slides.body: Standard self-attention is O(N²) in compute, but on modern GPUs the multiply-adds finish long before the data does. FlashAttention noticed that attention is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound — and got 2-4x faster by rewriting the same math to move less data, not do less of it.

slides.title: Materializing the Full Attention Matrix Is the Real Cost
bullets: Standard attention computes Q·Kᵀ, applies softmax, then multiplies by V — but the naive implementation writes the full N×N attention matrix (scores and post-softmax probabilities) out to GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at every step, then reads it back for the next op.

Modern GPUs have vastly more FLOPs available than memory bandwidth to feed them — for the small, repeated matrix operations in attention, the kernel spends most of its wall-clock time waiting on memory reads/writes, not doing arithmetic.

That N×N matrix also means quadratic memory: attention over a long sequence needs to hold a full sequence-length-squared matrix per head, per layer, which is what caps how long a context window standard attention can afford to train on.

This is a classic 'memory wall' problem — GPU compute has scaled much faster than memory bandwidth over the past decade, so kernels that were compute-bound in the past have quietly become bandwidth-bound.

slides.title: Tile the Computation, Never Materialize the Full Matrix
bullets: FlashAttention (Dao et al.) splits Q, K, V into small blocks that fit in the GPU's fast on-chip SRAM — orders of magnitude smaller but far faster than HBM — and fuses the matmul + softmax + matmul into a single kernel.

For each block, it computes partial attention scores and partial output entirely inside SRAM, then updates a running (unnormalized) output and running softmax statistics — never writing the full N×N score matrix to HBM at all.

This uses an 'online softmax' trick: because softmax needs a normalization constant over the whole row, FlashAttention keeps a running max and running sum per row and rescales previously-computed partial outputs as new blocks arrive, producing the mathematically exact same softmax as the standard two-pass version.

The result is exact attention — not an approximation like sparse or low-rank attention variants — with memory that scales linearly in sequence length instead of quadratically, because the full matrix is never stored.

slides.title: The Backward Pass Trades More FLOPs for Less I/O
bullets: Backpropagation normally needs the attention matrix computed in the forward pass — the naive approach is to store it, which is exactly the quadratic-memory cost FlashAttention just avoided.

Instead, FlashAttention recomputes the attention matrix on the fly during the backward pass, using the small saved softmax normalization statistics (the running max/sum from the forward pass) rather than reading a stored N×N matrix back from HBM.

This sounds like it should be slower — recomputation means strictly more floating-point operations than reusing a stored result. But because the kernel is bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound, avoiding the HBM read/write more than pays for the extra arithmetic.

This is the core IO-awareness idea: count HBM accesses, not just FLOPs, as the cost model — the standard implementation makes far more HBM accesses than FlashAttention for typical sequence lengths, and that gap is what drives the wall-clock speedup.

slides.title: Worked Example: Affording a Longer Context Window
slides.body: Say a training run needs to go from a 1K-token context to a 4K-token context — a 4x increase — on the same fixed GPU memory budget.
bullets: With standard attention, memory for the attention matrix grows with the square of sequence length, so a 4x longer context needs roughly 16x the attention memory per layer — on fixed GPU memory, that forces a much smaller batch size, or makes the run infeasible outright.

With FlashAttention's linear memory scaling, the same 4x context increase costs roughly 4x the memory, not 16x — leaving enough headroom to keep batch sizes practical instead of collapsing them to fit.

The original paper used exactly this kind of setup to train GPT-2 with a longer context than prior recipes on the same hardware, and reported the longer-context run reaching better quality — purely because the longer context became affordable to train on at all.

The same underlying fix produced two separate wins in that experiment: a roughly 2-4x wall-clock training speedup, and a context window that was out of reach for standard attention on the same hardware.

slides.title: Standard Attention vs. FlashAttention

rows: Never materialized — computed in tiles inside SRAM
Recomputes it from small saved statistics

slides.title: What It Doesn't Change, and Where It Gets Complicated
bullets: FlashAttention changes how attention is computed, not what it computes — it doesn't reduce the underlying quadratic FLOP count of full attention, so for extremely long sequences it's still doing quadratic work, just with far less wasted memory movement.

It's a hand-written, hardware-specific kernel — later versions (FlashAttention-2, FlashAttention-3) exist specifically because each new GPU generation has a different SRAM size, warp structure, and instruction set that needs re-tuning the tiling and scheduling to keep hitting close to peak throughput.

It doesn't help as much when a workload is already compute-bound rather than memory-bound — for very short sequences or unusual shapes where the N×N matrix was never the real bottleneck, the gain from avoiding HBM traffic shrinks.

For genuinely sub-quadratic scaling — not just less wasted memory within quadratic compute — you need a different algorithm entirely, such as state-space models like Mamba. FlashAttention makes exact quadratic attention efficient; it doesn't make attention linear-compute.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: FlashAttention is exact attention rewritten around the GPU memory hierarchy: tile Q/K/V into SRAM-sized blocks, fuse matmul+softmax+matmul into one kernel, and use online softmax so the full N×N matrix is never written to HBM.

That single change turns quadratic memory into linear memory, and — because attention on modern GPUs is bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound — trading extra backward-pass recomputation for less data movement makes the whole thing faster, not slower.
The reported system-level win was roughly a 2-4x training speedup plus the ability to train with meaningfully longer context on the same hardware, without changing the model's outputs at all.

It's an IO-aware systems optimization, not an approximation or a new architecture — which is why it composes with almost everything else (quantization, GQA, paged KV caches) rather than replacing them.

questions.prompt: What makes standard attention memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound on modern GPUs?
options: GPUs have too little compute to keep up with attention's FLOP count
The naive implementation writes/reads the full N×N attention matrix to/from HBM, and GPU memory bandwidth has grown much slower than compute
Softmax cannot be computed in parallel on a GPU
Attention requires more registers than a GPU streaming multiprocessor has available
questions.explanation: GPU compute (FLOPs) has scaled far faster than memory bandwidth over the past decade. The naive attention kernel repeatedly writes and reads the full N×N score/probability matrix to slow HBM, so it spends most of its time waiting on data movement rather than doing arithmetic — that's what 'memory-bandwidth bound' means.

questions.prompt: How does FlashAttention avoid quadratic memory growth while still computing exact softmax attention?
options: It approximates softmax with a cheaper linear function
It drops the lowest attention scores before computing softmax
It tiles Q/K/V into SRAM-sized blocks and uses a running max/sum (online softmax) to compute the exact result without ever storing the full N×N matrix
It caches the attention matrix from the previous layer and reuses it
questions.explanation: Online softmax lets FlashAttention process the sequence in tiles, keeping a running normalization statistic and rescaling partial outputs as new blocks arrive — mathematically identical to standard softmax, computed without ever materializing the full matrix.

questions.prompt: Why does recomputing the attention matrix during the backward pass make FlashAttention faster, not slower, despite doing more FLOPs?
options: Recomputation runs on a separate, otherwise-idle GPU
GPUs have compute capacity to spare relative to memory bandwidth, so avoiding a large HBM read/write more than offsets the extra arithmetic
The backward pass doesn't actually need the attention matrix at all
Recomputation only happens during inference, not training
questions.explanation: This is the IO-awareness core idea: on a bandwidth-bound kernel, the real cost is HBM traffic, not FLOP count. Recomputing from small saved statistics avoids a large HBM read of the stored matrix, and since GPUs have compute to spare relative to bandwidth, that trade comes out ahead in wall-clock time.

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Ahead, Verifying in Parallel
posts.subtitle: How a small draft model lets a big model check several tokens at once
posts.summary: Autoregressive decoding generates one token per full forward pass through the model, which wastes the GPU's compute because each pass is bottlenecked on moving weights from memory, not on the math itself. Speculative decoding fixes this by having a small, fast draft model guess several tokens ahead, then having the big model verify that whole guess in a single parallel pass — accepting whatever the draft got right and only paying the big model's full cost once per batch of guesses, without changing a single output token.

slides.title: The GPU Is Waiting, Not Computing
slides.body: Generating a reply token by token means running a full forward pass through every layer of the model for each token. On modern GPUs, that pass is bottlenecked by moving billions of weight values out of memory, not by the arithmetic — so most of the GPU's compute capacity sits idle during ordinary decoding.

slides.title: Decoding Is Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound
bullets: Each decode step reads the entire model's weights from GPU memory to produce exactly one token — for a large model that's tens of gigabytes moved per token, every token
The actual matrix multiplications for a single new token are cheap; the GPU's compute units finish almost instantly and then sit idle waiting on memory bandwidth
This means decoding one token or verifying several tokens in parallel costs roughly the same wall-clock time — the bottleneck is the weight transfer, which happens once either way
That gap between 'compute available' and 'compute used' is exactly what speculative decoding spends

slides.title: A Cheap Model Guesses, the Big Model Checks the Whole Guess at Once
bullets: A small, fast 'draft' model — often a distilled or much smaller version of the target model — generates K candidate tokens autoregressively, one at a time, which is cheap because it's a small model

The large 'target' model then runs a single forward pass over all K draft tokens simultaneously, since verifying K positions in parallel costs about the same as generating one token alone (the process is memory-bound, not compute-bound)

The target model compares its own predicted distribution at each position against the draft's chosen token: it accepts tokens left-to-right as long as they'd plausibly be sampled by the target model too

At the first position where they diverge, the draft token is rejected and replaced with a token resampled from a corrected distribution — everything after that point is thrown away and re-guessed next round

slides.title: Worked Example: Four Guesses, Three Survive
slides.body: The draft model proposes the continuation "the cat sat down" as four tokens: "the", "cat", "sat", "down".
bullets: The target model verifies all four in one parallel pass and agrees with 'the', 'cat', and 'sat' — those tokens are accepted exactly as the draft wrote them, no extra cost
At 'down', the target model's own distribution favors 'quietly' instead — the draft is rejected here, and a replacement token is sampled from the target's corrected distribution at that position
Net result: 4 tokens produced (3 accepted + 1 resampled) for the price of one target-model forward pass plus four cheap draft-model steps — versus 4 full target-model passes under ordinary decoding
If the draft had matched all four, the round would produce 4 tokens for the same one-pass cost — the speedup scales directly with how often the draft agrees with the target

slides.title: Why the Output Is Provably Identical
bullets: The acceptance rule isn't a heuristic filter — it's a form of rejection sampling constructed so the accepted-or-resampled token has exactly the same probability distribution as sampling directly from the target model alone
This makes speculative decoding lossless: the final text you get has the same distribution as running the expensive target model by itself, token by token, with no draft model at all
That guarantee is the whole reason labs are comfortable shipping it in production — it's a pure latency optimization, not a quality tradeoff or an approximation
It only speeds up generation; it does nothing for the model's reasoning, knowledge, or accuracy — a wrong answer decoded speculatively is still exactly as wrong as decoded normally

slides.title: Where the 'Draft' Comes From

rows: A smaller model from the same family (e.g. a distilled variant)
Best acceptance rates, but needs a second model loaded and maintained
The target model itself, exited early at a middle layer
No second model to manage, but drafts are lower quality than a purpose-trained one
Additional lightweight heads attached to the target model's last layer
One model to deploy, but requires extra training of the heads
Matches from the prompt or a static corpus, no model at all
Nearly free to run, but only helps when the continuation echoes existing text

slides.title: When It Barely Helps — or Isn't Worth the Complexity
bullets: The speedup is capped by how often the draft agrees with the target — highly creative, open-ended, or unpredictable text gives the draft little to correctly guess, so acceptance rates (and the payoff) drop
Gains shrink as batch size grows: decoding many sequences at once is already closer to compute-bound, so there's less idle GPU capacity left for speculative verification to soak up
It adds real operational cost — a second model (or extra heads) to host, tune the guess length K for, and keep in sync with the target model as it's updated
Picking K too high wastes draft-model compute on tokens that will likely be rejected anyway; picking it too low leaves speedup on the table — it typically needs tuning per workload

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Ordinary decoding wastes GPU compute because moving weights from memory, not arithmetic, is the bottleneck — verifying several tokens costs about the same as generating one

A cheap draft model proposes several tokens ahead; the expensive target model verifies them all in a single parallel pass and accepts whatever a correctly-constructed rejection-sampling rule would have produced anyway
The technique is lossless — output distribution matches running the target model alone — so it's a pure latency win, not a quality tradeoff
It pays off most on predictable text and small batches, and pays off least on highly creative generation or already-compute-bound, high-batch serving

questions.prompt: Why does verifying 4 draft tokens in one target-model pass cost about the same as generating 1 token normally?
options: The target model skips most of its layers during verification
Decoding is bottlenecked by moving weights from memory, which happens once per pass regardless of how many token positions are processed in that pass
Draft tokens don't need to go through the target model's attention layers
GPUs can only process one model at a time, so the draft model pauses while verification runs
questions.explanation: Ordinary decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: the cost is dominated by streaming the model's weights out of memory, not by the matrix math for one extra token. Processing several token positions in one forward pass reuses that same memory transfer, so the marginal compute cost is small.

questions.prompt: What guarantees that speculative decoding doesn't change the quality or content of the output compared to normal decoding?
options: The draft model is fine-tuned to always match the target model exactly
Rejected tokens are simply skipped, shortening the response slightly
The accept/resample rule is constructed as rejection sampling so the resulting token distribution exactly matches sampling from the target model alone
Only draft tokens with high confidence scores above a fixed threshold are ever proposed
questions.explanation: Speculative decoding's acceptance test is a rejection-sampling scheme, not a heuristic: it's mathematically constructed so that the final sampled token — whether accepted from the draft or resampled at a mismatch — has the same probability distribution as decoding directly from the target model. That's what makes it lossless.

questions.prompt: In which scenario does speculative decoding provide the LEAST speedup?
options: Serving a single request with a highly predictable continuation, like completing a common phrase
Generating highly creative, unpredictable text at a large batch size where GPUs are already compute-bound
Autocompleting boilerplate code with a strong draft model
Any workload, since speculative decoding always gives the same fixed speedup
questions.explanation: Two effects compound against speculative decoding here: unpredictable text makes the draft model guess wrong more often, and large batches push decoding toward being compute-bound rather than memory-bound — the idle GPU capacity that speculative verification exploits is exactly what shrinks at high batch sizes.

posts.title: Agent Memory: What Survives the Session, What Doesn't
posts.subtitle: The context window forgets everything on the next call. Memory is the system you bolt on so it doesn't.
posts.summary: LLMs are stateless — every call starts from zero unless you feed prior context back in. Agent memory is the engineering layer that decides what gets kept, how it's stored, and how it's found again, trading cost and staleness risk for continuity across sessions.

slides.title: The Model Never Remembers — Something Else Has To
slides.body: Every LLM call is stateless: swap in a fresh context window and the model has no idea a previous conversation ever happened. Agent memory is the layer that captures, stores, and re-injects what matters.

slides.title: Stuffing the Whole Transcript Back In Doesn't Scale
slides.body: The naive fix — replay the full conversation history every call — works until it doesn't.
bullets: A context window is finite (even a 200K-token one); a long-running agent with weeks of history will eventually overflow it.
Cost scales with every token you re-send: a 50K-token history replayed on every turn means paying to re-read it 50K times over a long session.
Attention dilutes across a long, mostly-irrelevant transcript — the one fact that matters ('user's API key is stored in vault X') gets buried under thousands of tokens of small talk.

slides.title: Three Layers, Borrowed From How People Remember
slides.body: Agent memory systems typically separate what's needed right now from what's worth keeping forever.
bullets: Working memory: the current context window — the live scratchpad for this task, gone once the call ends unless captured elsewhere.
Episodic memory: a log of past interactions or sessions ('on Tuesday, the user asked to refactor the auth module') — useful for continuity, not for facts.
Semantic memory: durable facts extracted out of episodes ('user prefers tabs, not spaces'; 'user's default cloud is AWS') — small, stable, and cheap to re-inject every turn.

slides.title: Four Ways to Implement It, in Increasing Complexity
slides.body: Each approach makes a different tradeoff between simplicity, cost, and how much history it can hold.
bullets: Full transcript in context: simplest, zero infra, but hits the context ceiling and gets expensive fast — fine for short-lived agents only.
Periodic summarization/compaction: an LLM call condenses old turns into a shorter summary before they fall out of the window — bounded cost, but detail is lossy and irreversible.

Vector store + retrieval: embed past interactions or facts, retrieve the top-k most relevant to the current turn — scales to unbounded history, adds embedding + search latency and a new failure mode (retrieving the wrong thing).

Structured key-value facts: extract discrete facts into a small structured store (a user-preferences table, not free text) — the cheapest to re-inject and the easiest to audit or correct, but only captures what you explicitly designed a field for.

slides.title: A Coding Assistant Across Three Sessions
slides.body: Session 1: the user tells the agent 'I use 2-space indentation, and never touch the migrations folder.' Session 2, a week later, opens with a blank context window.
bullets: With no memory: the agent reformats the user's next file with 4 spaces and happily edits a migration — both facts are gone.

With semantic memory: at session start, the agent retrieves two structured facts ('indent: 2-space', 'do-not-touch: /migrations') and injects them into the fresh context — about 20 tokens, not 20,000.

With vector-store episodic memory: the agent instead retrieves the top-3 most similar past turns to the current request, which works for fuzzier context but can surface an outdated or half-relevant snippet instead of the clean fact.

slides.title: Picking a Strategy by What You're Optimizing For

rows: High, but only for modeled fields

slides.title: Pitfalls: Stale Facts, Hallucinated Memory, and Leakage
slides.body: Memory doesn't remove failure modes — it introduces new ones on top of whatever the base agent already has.
bullets: Stale contradiction: the user says 'actually, switch to 4-space indentation' in session 3 — if the old fact isn't overwritten, the agent now has two conflicting 'truths' and no way to know which is current.
Hallucinated memory: a summarization step can compress two unrelated facts into one plausible-sounding but false statement, which then gets treated as ground truth on every future turn.

Cross-session leakage: a shared vector store across users/tenants without strict namespacing can retrieve one user's private facts into another user's context — a correctness bug that's also a security incident.
When NOT to bother: single-shot tasks with no follow-up ('summarize this PDF') gain nothing from persistent memory and just add latency and attack surface for no benefit.

slides.title: Memory Is a Storage Decision, Not a Model Feature
slides.body: The LLM itself never remembers anything — every strategy above is plumbing you build around it.
bullets: Default to structured facts for anything you can name in advance (preferences, constraints); reach for vector retrieval only for the fuzzier, unstructured long-tail.
Every memory write needs an update/overwrite path, or contradictions silently accumulate until the agent is confidently wrong.
Treat memory retrieval as untrusted input, same as any RAG chunk — a bad or leaked retrieval can steer the agent as badly as a bad prompt.

questions.prompt: Why can't an agent just replay the full conversation transcript on every call to 'remember' everything?
options: LLMs reject any input longer than one sentence
The context window is finite and cost scales with every token re-sent, so a long-running history eventually overflows or becomes too expensive
Transcripts are encrypted and can't be re-read
It works fine and is the recommended approach for any agent
questions.explanation: Context windows are large but finite, and every re-sent token is paid for again — a week-long agent session can't just keep appending its full history forever without hitting a wall on both length and cost.

questions.prompt: A user tells an agent 'switch to 4-space indentation' after previously saying 'use 2-space.' What failure mode does this risk if memory isn't handled carefully?
options: The agent will refuse to respond at all
A stale contradiction — the old fact isn't overwritten, so the agent has two conflicting 'truths' with no signal for which is current
The context window will physically corrupt
This has no effect on agent behavior
questions.explanation: Without an explicit update/overwrite path, a memory store just accumulates facts. When two entries conflict, the agent has no principled way to know the newer one should win.

questions.prompt: Why should retrieved memories be treated as untrusted input, similar to a RAG chunk?
options: Because memory retrieval is always slower than a fresh LLM call
Because a bad, stale, or cross-tenant-leaked retrieval can steer the agent just as badly as a bad prompt, so it needs the same scrutiny
Because vector stores cannot store text, only numbers
Because memories are never actually used by the model
questions.explanation: A retrieved memory is injected straight into the context the model reasons over — if it's wrong, stale, or belongs to a different user, it influences the agent's output exactly like any other untrusted context, including RAG chunks.

posts.title: HNSW: The Graph That Makes Vector Search Fast
posts.subtitle: Skip lists for vectors: finding your nearest neighbor in log-time, not linear time.
posts.summary: Exact nearest-neighbor search means comparing a query against every stored vector — fine for thousands, unusable for millions. HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph that turns that linear scan into a logarithmic graph walk, trading a small, tunable amount of recall for the speedup that makes real-time RAG retrieval possible.

slides.title: Nearest-Neighbor Search Doesn't Have to Touch Every Vector
slides.body: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph-based index behind most production vector databases — Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, and FAISS all ship it. It turns a linear scan into a logarithmic graph walk.

slides.title: Brute-Force kNN Is Linear — and RAG Can't Afford That
slides.body: The exact way to find a query's nearest neighbors is to compute its distance to every stored vector and sort. That's O(n·d) per query — n vectors, d dimensions.
bullets: At 100K embeddings this is a few milliseconds; at 50M it's seconds per query — too slow for a retrieval step inside an interactive chat response.
Every added document makes every future query proportionally slower, since there's nothing to skip — you always compare against everything.
The fix has to be approximate: give up the guarantee of finding the exact top-k in exchange for sub-linear search time.

slides.title: HNSW Stacks Sparse-to-Dense Graph Layers Like a Skip List
slides.body: Each vector is inserted into a multi-layer graph — always on layer 0, and on each layer above with exponentially decaying probability, so the top layer has only a handful of points.
bullets: Search starts at a single entry point on the sparsest top layer and greedily hops to whichever neighbor is closest to the query.
When no neighbor at the current layer is closer, the walk drops down one layer and keeps hopping — sparse top layers cover long distances fast, lower layers refine locally.
By layer 0, the walk has narrowed to a small neighborhood of true near-neighbors, checked in roughly O(log n) hops instead of comparing against all n.

slides.title: Three Knobs Trade Recall Against Speed and Memory
bullets: M — max connections per node per layer (typically 16-64). Higher M means a denser, more accurate graph but more memory and slower inserts.
efConstruction — candidate list size while building the graph. Higher values build a better-connected graph at the cost of slower indexing, a one-time cost paid at insert.
efSearch — candidate list size at query time. This is the one knob you can turn per request without rebuilding the index: higher efSearch trades latency for recall.
A typical starting point is M=16, efConstruction=200, with efSearch tuned per workload somewhere between 50 and 200.

slides.title: HNSW vs Flat vs IVF, by the Property That Matters

rows: Depends on nprobe; drops if clusters are lopsided
Needs a training pass to fit cluster centroids
Vectors + M links per layer per node — often 1.5-2x raw vector size

slides.title: 5M Document Chunks, One Query, Two Very Different Costs
slides.body: A RAG system embeds 5 million 768-dimension chunks from a document corpus. A user question arrives as a single query vector.
bullets: Brute-force: the query is compared against all 5,000,000 vectors, computing 5M similarity ops before returning the top-5.
HNSW: the walk touches a few thousand candidate nodes total across all layers — a handful of long jumps at the top, then a bounded local search at layer 0 — before returning a near-identical top-5.

Both approaches typically return the same or near-same top-5 chunks — the difference is the number of comparisons needed to find them, which is what separates a retrieval step that fits inside a tight latency budget from one that doesn't.

slides.title: Where HNSW Costs You: Memory, Deletes, and Guarantees
slides.body: The speed isn't free — three real tradeoffs show up in production.
bullets: No recall guarantee: HNSW is approximate by construction — a badly tuned efSearch can silently miss true nearest neighbors with no error thrown.
Deletes are expensive: most implementations don't support true node removal — they tombstone the entry and still traverse through it, so delete-heavy workloads need periodic full rebuilds.

Memory scales with M: storing graph edges, not just vectors, means an HNSW index can use noticeably more RAM than a flat index of the same vectors — a real constraint at hundreds of millions of vectors.

When NOT to use it: small collections (under roughly 10-50K vectors) where a flat scan is already fast enough and simpler to reason about, or use cases requiring guaranteed exact recall — like legal or compliance search — where approximate results aren't acceptable.

slides.title: Approximate, Tunable, and the Default for a Reason
slides.body: HNSW trades a small, controllable amount of recall for a massive drop in query cost — exactly the trade most RAG systems want.
bullets: The core idea is a multi-layer graph: sparse layers for long jumps, dense layers for local refinement — the same trick a skip list uses for sorted lists, applied to vector space.
M and efConstruction are build-time decisions; efSearch is the dial you turn per query to trade latency for recall without touching the index.
Reach for HNSW when queries are frequent and latency-sensitive; reach for a flat index when the collection is small or exact results are non-negotiable.

questions.prompt: Why is brute-force k-nearest-neighbor search a poor fit for RAG retrieval over millions of embeddings?
options: It requires a GPU to compute cosine similarity
It compares the query against every stored vector, so query time grows linearly with the collection size
It can only be used with normalized vectors
It doesn't support cosine similarity, only Euclidean distance
questions.explanation: Brute-force kNN is O(n·d) per query — every stored vector must be compared. That's fine at 100K vectors but becomes seconds-per-query at tens of millions, too slow for an interactive retrieval step.

questions.prompt: In HNSW, what does raising efSearch at query time actually trade off?
options: It rebuilds the graph with more connections per node
It widens the candidate list explored during search, trading latency for higher recall
It reduces the number of layers in the graph
It changes the distance metric used for comparison
questions.explanation: efSearch controls how many candidates are kept in the search frontier at query time — no index rebuild required. A higher value explores more of the graph, catching more true nearest neighbors at the cost of a slower query.

questions.prompt: Why is deleting a vector from an HNSW index harder than deleting a row from a flat array?
options: HNSW vectors are stored in a read-only format
Other nodes' edges may route through the deleted node during traversal, so most implementations tombstone it and reclaim space via periodic rebuilds rather than removing it immediately
Deletes are actually just as cheap as with a flat index
HNSW doesn't allow inserts either, so it's built once and never changes
questions.explanation: The graph's connectivity depends on every node's links, so cleanly removing one requires re-routing its neighbors' edges. Most implementations avoid that cost per-delete by marking it deleted (skipped in results, still traversed) and periodically rebuilding.

posts.title: Event-Driven Architecture: Systems That React Instead of Ask
posts.subtitle: Why Kafka, SQS, and EventBridge exist, and what they cost you.
posts.summary: Request/response chains couple every service's uptime to the slowest link and force producers to know every future consumer. Event-driven architecture routes events through a broker instead, decoupling services at the cost of immediate consistency and a single call stack to debug.

slides.title: Producers Emit, Consumers React — Nobody Calls Anybody
slides.body: Event-driven architecture replaces direct service-to-service calls with asynchronous events flowing through a broker, trading immediate consistency for independence and resilience.

slides.title: Synchronous Call Chains Couple Every Service's Uptime Together
slides.body: In a request/response architecture, Service A calling B calling C means A is only as available and as fast as the slowest link in that chain.
bullets: If C is down or slow, B's request blocks or times out, and A's request blocks behind it — one failure cascades backward through the whole chain.
Adding a new consumer of A's data (say, a fraud-check service) means changing A's code to call it directly, coupling A to every future subscriber.
Scaling requires every service in the chain to scale together, even when only one of them is the actual bottleneck.

slides.title: A Broker Sits Between Producers and Consumers
slides.body: Instead of calling other services directly, a service publishes an event (e.g. OrderPlaced) to a broker — Kafka, SQS, EventBridge, RabbitMQ. Any number of consumers subscribe independently.
bullets: The producer doesn't know or care who — or how many — consumers exist; it writes the event and moves on.
Consumers process events at their own pace, so a slow or down consumer doesn't block the producer or any other consumer.
Most brokers guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once, so a message can arrive more than once during retries.

slides.title: Choreography vs Orchestration: Who Decides What Happens Next
slides.body: There are two ways to coordinate a multi-step workflow across services that communicate through events.
bullets: Choreography: each service reacts to events and emits its own — OrderPlaced triggers Inventory to reserve stock and emit StockReserved, which triggers Payment. No single service knows the whole flow.
Orchestration: a central coordinator (e.g. Temporal, AWS Step Functions) calls each step explicitly and tracks the overall workflow state.
Choreography scales better and has no single point of control; orchestration keeps 'why did this order fail' answerable in one place instead of scattered across every consumer's logs.

slides.title: Request/Response vs Event-Driven, by the Property That Matters

rows: Caller must know callee's address & API
Producer knows only the event schema
Callee down means caller blocks or fails
Callee down means events queue until it recovers
Subscribe to the topic; zero producer changes
Spread across every consumer's own logs

slides.title: One Order, Three Independent Consumers
slides.body: An e-commerce checkout service publishes a single OrderPlaced event carrying order ID, items, and total.
bullets: The Inventory service consumes it to decrement stock and, if a SKU is out, emits an OutOfStock event — checkout never needed to know Inventory exists.
The Notification service consumes the same event to send a confirmation email, added six months after launch by subscribing to the existing topic with zero changes to checkout's code.
The Analytics pipeline consumes it into a warehouse for revenue dashboards — a third consumer, again with no coordination required between teams.

slides.title: Pitfalls: Duplicates, Ordering, and the Poison Message
slides.body: Decoupling doesn't remove the hard problems — it relocates them to the consumer.
bullets: At-least-once delivery means consumers MUST be idempotent — processing the same OrderPlaced event twice must not charge the customer twice.
Ordering is only guaranteed within a partition (Kafka) or not at all (SQS standard queues); cross-service ordering needs a shared partition key like order ID.
A malformed 'poison' message a consumer can't process will loop on retries and block that consumer's queue unless routed to a dead-letter queue after a max-retry count.
When NOT to use it: a workflow needing an immediate synchronous answer — 'is this credit card valid right now' — is a poor fit; event-driven trades away that immediacy for decoupling.

slides.title: Decoupling Is the Point, Eventual Consistency Is the Cost
slides.body: Event-driven architecture isn't free — it's a trade.
bullets: Producers and consumers no longer share deployment schedules, uptime, or scaling needs — new consumers subscribe without touching producer code.
In exchange, you give up immediate consistency and a single call stack to debug, and take on idempotency, ordering, and dead-letter handling as first-class design problems.
Reach for it when consumers are numerous, independent, or unknown at design time; reach for direct calls when you need an answer right now.

questions.prompt: Why must consumers in most event-driven systems be idempotent?
options: Because brokers process events in random order
Because most brokers guarantee at-least-once delivery, so a consumer can receive the same event more than once
Because events are always broadcast to every consumer
Because idempotency is required by the HTTP spec
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery (the default in systems like Kafka and SQS) means retries can redeliver a message that was already processed, so handling it twice must be safe — e.g. checking an order ID before charging again.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between choreography and orchestration in event-driven workflows?
options: Choreography is synchronous, orchestration is asynchronous
Choreography has each service react to events independently; orchestration uses a central coordinator that explicitly calls each step
Orchestration doesn't use a message broker
They are two names for the same pattern
questions.explanation: In choreography, no single service knows the full workflow — each just reacts to events and emits its own. Orchestration centralizes that knowledge in a coordinator, trading a single point of control for easier tracing.

questions.prompt: A consumer keeps crashing on one malformed event, retrying forever and blocking the rest of its queue. What's the standard fix?
options: Delete the broker and restart
Route the message to a dead-letter queue after a maximum retry count, so it stops blocking healthy messages
Have the producer stop sending any events
Increase the retry count to infinity
questions.explanation: A dead-letter queue isolates messages that repeatedly fail processing (a 'poison message') after N retries, letting the rest of the queue keep flowing while the bad message is inspected separately.

posts.title: ToolHazard: Scaling Adversarial Environments for Agent Security
posts.subtitle: Hand-built red-team environments don't scale. ToolHazard synthesizes stateful ones automatically — and shows agents are still very easy to hijack.
posts.summary: ToolHazard is a framework that auto-generates stateful, tool-using environments to stress-test LLM agents against indirect prompt injection, replacing the manually-built or LLM-simulated environments prior security benchmarks relied on. Its ToolHazard-Bench (87 long-horizon tasks, 28 environments, 512 tools) shows agents remain highly vulnerable, that injection timing/placement changes attack success, and that training on ToolHazard-generated attacks measurably improves security on both ToolHazard-Bench and the existing AgentDojo benchmark without hurting benign task performance.

slides.title: The Attack Doesn't Come From the User — It Comes From the Tool Output
slides.body: An agent that reads a webpage, a file, or an API response is trusting that content as much as it trusts its own instructions. Indirect prompt injection hides an attack inside exactly that content.

slides.title: Security Benchmarks Were the Bottleneck, Not the Attacks
bullets: Testing agent security at scale needs realistic, stateful environments — a fake email inbox, a fake shell, a fake ticketing system the agent can actually act on, not just a static prompt.

Prior work mostly relied on manually implemented or reused environments (slow, doesn't scale to new domains), or stochastic LLM-simulated tools (inconsistent, hard to reproduce), with injection points chosen in advance by the researchers.
That combination caps how broad and how realistic security evaluation can get — you can't stress-test an agent against attack surfaces nobody thought to hand-build.
ToolHazard's contribution isn't a new attack technique — it's a way to generate the adversarial environments themselves at scale, so evaluation can cover far more ground automatically.

slides.title: Three Roles Synthesize an Attack End-to-End
bullets: Environment Simulator: builds an executable, stateful environment (tools + underlying state) from a seed domain — so the agent's actions have real, persistent consequences, not scripted responses.
Attacker Agent: automatically discovers viable injection points inside that environment and generates payloads specific to it, instead of reusing a generic injected string across every domain.
User Simulator: constructs state-grounded, long-horizon tasks — multi-step goals that give the injected payload realistic opportunities to be encountered during normal tool use.
Together these three roles remove the human-engineering bottleneck: new seed domains and more compute directly buy more coverage, instead of more researcher-hours per environment.

slides.title: ToolHazard-Bench at a Glance
slides.body: The benchmark built from this framework is substantially larger and more complex than prior hand-built agent security suites.

slides.title: Worked Example: Where the Payload Lands Matters
bullets: Picture an agent working a long-horizon task: read a support ticket, check an internal wiki, then send a reply — five or six tool calls deep.

The paper's findings show attacks are more effective when the injected instruction is encountered EARLIER in that sequence, and when it's placed near the END of a given tool observation (e.g. the tail of a long wiki page) rather than buried in the middle.

That means the same malicious string can succeed or fail purely based on where in the task and where in the document it's positioned — timing and placement are attack variables on their own, independent of the payload's content.
For anyone building agent evals, this implies a single injection test at a single position badly undersells real risk — you need to vary position and timing to see the actual attack surface.

slides.title: The Headline Result: Agents Are Still Easy to Hijack
bullets: Finding 1: LLM agents remain highly vulnerable to environmental prompt injections — this holds across the framework's generated environments, not just a handful of hand-picked cases.
Finding 2: injection timing and placement measurably change attack effectiveness (see the worked example) — defenses that only pattern-match on payload content will miss this dimension entirely.

Finding 3: training/alignment using ToolHazard-generated attack data improves security on BOTH ToolHazard-Bench and the pre-existing AgentDojo benchmark — evidence the generated attacks aren't just overfitting to their own benchmark.
Critically, that security improvement held while preserving benign task utility — the fix isn't just making the agent refuse more often at the cost of usefulness.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: ToolHazard automates building the stateful, tool-using environments needed for agent security testing — the bottleneck it removes is environment construction, not attack invention.
ToolHazard-Bench (87 tasks, 28 environments, 512 tools) is bigger and more realistic than prior hand-built agent security benchmarks.
Attack success depends on injection timing and placement, not just payload content — evaluation and defenses both need to account for position, not only text-matching.
Training on ToolHazard-generated attacks transferred to an independent benchmark (AgentDojo) without hurting benign performance — a meaningful signal the approach generalizes.

questions.prompt: What is ToolHazard's main contribution, according to the paper?
options: A brand-new prompt injection attack technique nobody had used before
A framework that automatically synthesizes stateful, tool-using adversarial environments at scale, instead of relying on hand-built or LLM-simulated ones
A patch that fully eliminates prompt injection vulnerability in LLM agents
A dataset of only static, single-turn text prompts
questions.explanation: ToolHazard's contribution is scaling environment construction itself — via an Environment Simulator, Attacker Agent, and User Simulator — so security evaluation can cover far more realistic, stateful domains than manually engineered benchmarks allowed.

questions.prompt: According to the paper's findings, what makes an injected instruction MORE likely to succeed?
options: Being encountered later in the task and placed at the very start of an observation
Being encountered earlier in the task and placed near the end of an observation
Injection timing and placement have no measurable effect on success
Only using injections written in a different language than the task
questions.explanation: The paper found attacks are more effective when injected instructions are encountered earlier in a long-horizon task and positioned near the end of a given tool observation — both position and timing are real attack-effectiveness variables.

questions.prompt: How did the paper demonstrate that alignment using ToolHazard-generated attacks actually generalizes, rather than just overfitting?
options: By showing security gains only appear on ToolHazard-Bench itself
By showing the security improvement transferred to AgentDojo, an independent pre-existing benchmark, while preserving benign task utility
By testing on a single hand-picked example and declaring success
The paper doesn't test generalization at all
questions.explanation: Training on ToolHazard-generated attack data improved security on both ToolHazard-Bench and the separate AgentDojo benchmark, without degrading performance on benign tasks — evidence the defense isn't just narrowly fit to ToolHazard's own test set.
